meta.confidence: good evidence, poor convergence — the most contested boundary on the ladder, and the most conservatively scored of the four steps built so far

confidence_source.cites: "Reasonable industry coverage with real but modest internal disagreement on exact hours (75 vs 100 vs 100+). This is the step where sub-class fuzziness (high-B vs low-C overlap) is most clearly documented, so the app should be most cautious about hard EN-letter gating right here." The step file opens by calling this "arguably the most contested boundary on the entire ladder — the community itself debates whether it's even meaningful".
confidence_source.note: IMPORTANT: this is a DIFFERENT kind of uncertainty from config/scoring/low-b-to-mid-b.json's, and the pilot-facing copy must not reuse that step's language. There, the problem is that almost nobody wrote about the boundary ('low — the lowest of any step built so far'). Here there is more material than at any rung below — industry hours figures, two official pilot-rating ladders, four expert podcast voices, named manufacturer positioning — and it does not converge: Flybubble's own two articles give 75 and 100 hours, 406 Paragliding gives 100+, Passion Paragliding gives 70 hours a year, the community rule of thumb is 50 a year, and Nova markets its entry C as 'a small step' from its benchmark high-B. Compare config/scoring/a-to-low-b.json ('comparatively high for this step'), config/scoring/low-b-to-mid-b.json ('low — thin evidence') and config/scoring/mid-b-to-high-b.json ('moderate-to-good'). The honest one-line summary for this step is 'plenty of guidance that argues with itself', and that is what meta.confidence_statement_for_ui in config/questions/high-b-to-low-c.json says.

design_decisions.change: The two forces at this boundary pull in apparently opposite directions and were resolved by separating them: fuzzy, non-converging evidence governs METHOD (what may be gated on, and at what distance from any published figure), while the asymmetric-risk finding governs LEVEL (where the Ready bar, the category floors and the Ready-blocker list sit). Concretely: no gate sits at any source's actual hours figure, and the unconditional hours gate sits at a THIRD of the lowest published reading — but thresholds.ready.total_min rises to 78 (from 76 one rung down), the Ready category floors rise to 72/68 (from 70/65), critical_check_floor gains a tenth member and bites a band higher on four questions, and a new combination gate caps a pilot whose collapse response is entirely unevidenced.
design_decisions.reason: Both findings are real and both are in the same step file. The fuzziness is documented in the source-quality note and knowledge/disagreements.md points 2, 3 and 6. The asymmetry is documented twice, in two different currencies: the forum consensus that "the penalty for choosing a C when you should be on a B can be rather more severe than the penalty for flying a B when you should have gone for a C", and the financial version — EN-C wings hold resale value worse, so an unnecessary C purchase is an expensive mistake where an unnecessary B purchase rarely is. Treating fuzzy evidence as a reason to be LENIENT would be the wrong inference: not knowing exactly where the line is, at a boundary where the sources themselves say err on the cautious side, argues for standing further back from it, not for stepping over it.
design_decisions.what_this_costs: A borderline pilot who would have reached Ready one rung down on an equivalent answer profile will often land at Nearly ready here. That is intended. The cost is explicitly NOT paid in more Not yet results: thresholds.nearly_ready.total_min is held at 55, identical to all three steps below, so the extra strictness sits entirely on the Ready edge, in the gates and in the harder per-option scores.

source.cites: "The community consensus captured in the paraglidingforum thread is blunt about the asymmetry of risk... i.e., sources agree err on the side of caution at this specific boundary more than at earlier ones." Plus the psychological section: "EN-C wings hold resale value worse than B wings, and 'buying a C can be a very expensive mistake' if the pilot isn't ready, while an unnecessary B purchase rarely is — an asymmetric-downside argument that supports a cautious gate at this step."
source.note: knowledge/disagreements.md point 5's conservative-by-default pattern (borrowed from SAHPA defaulting an unregistered glider to the most demanding category) is the tie-breaker that makes this resolution consistent with the rest of the knowledge base rather than a one-off judgement.

design_decisions.change: The six in-air and collapse-handling questions (active_piloting 13, thermal_turn_control 12, collapse_practice 12, reading_the_day 11, collapse_experience 10, conditions_flown 10) carry 68 of the 198 skills weight, 34%. The two currency questions (airtime_last_12m 11, flying_frequency 11) carry 22, 11%. The three purely cumulative questions (total_airtime 7, total_flights 5, current_wing_time 7) carry 19, under 10%. thermic_airtime, the single best-sourced number at this step, carries 15 — the highest single skills weight, but less than a twelfth of the category.
design_decisions.reason: Same shape as low-B to mid-B, for a different reason, and the difference matters. There, demonstrated skill outweighed hours because the hours evidence was thin and probably an outlier. Here it outweighs hours because knowledge/disagreements.md point 3 names THIS boundary as the one where the class labels least reliably predict how demanding a specific wing is, and recommends in terms: "Weight the pilot's self-reported skills, conditions flown, and collapse-recovery comfort more heavily than 'which sub-class is the current wing' at the fuzzy boundaries (especially high-B/low-C)." knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md adds a second, independent expert voice for the same conclusion — Greg Hamerton, explicit that the EN/AFNOR letter on its own doesn't tell a pilot how often a given wing actually collapses — and Seb Ospina's reframe gives the positive version: the EN-C step is where a wing starts transmitting genuinely useful extra information about the air, which is only worth anything to a pilot who can already read it.

source.cites: Recommended handling, quoted above. Reinforced by knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#psychological--mindset-factors: the "High End Bs vs. Low EN Cs" thread shows pilots disagreeing about which actually feels calmer in bad air, which "argues for the app weighting the pilot's own reported comfort/control in rough air fairly heavily at this step, rather than leaning only on the EN letter."
source.note: That last sentence is also why response_when_rough carries 15, the highest single weight in the whole rubric, skills or psychological.

design_decisions.change: total_airtime, total_flights, thermic_airtime, airtime_last_12m and current_wing_time keep config/questions/mid-b-to-high-b.json's exact bands, so all five merge into a single screen in a chained run. Only the scores attached to those bands change, and they change substantially: 25-50 thermic hours scores 0.6 at mid-B to high-B and 0.3 here.
design_decisions.reason: The parent decision at mid-B to high-B was to introduce thermic_airtime as its own question because every hours source there measured thermic flying. Every hours source HERE measures thermic flying too (Flybubble 100, Flybubble 75, 406 Paragliding 100+), so the same question is the right one and re-banding it would have produced a near-duplicate screen for no evidential gain. knowledge/disagreements.md point 2 instructs broad bands rather than any single source's precise figure, which is an argument against inventing a 75-hour boundary that only one of the two Flybubble articles supports.
design_decisions.what_this_costs: Two real straddles, recorded rather than hidden. (1) The 50-100 thermic band contains both published readings (75 and 100), so a pilot in it may be below both or above the lower one, and the rubric cannot tell. It scores 0.6 — passing the Ready-blocker, well short of full marks — which is the honest value for a band the evidence cannot resolve. (2) The 150-300 flights band straddles USHPA P4's 250-flight figure. total_flights is weight 5 and gates nothing, so that straddle costs almost nothing. Both are listed in meta.owner_decisions as re-bandable if the owner would rather have precision than a merged screen.

source.cites: "Use broad bands (e.g. 'tens of hours', 'roughly 50-100', '100+ per year ongoing') rather than picking one source's precise figure, and weight recent/currency hours independently from total hours." Also the specific entry for this step: "High-B → low-C: Flybubble gives 100 hours cumulative in one article and 75 hours cumulative in another (same retailer, different articles)."
source.note: BRIEF.md's 'Multi-step jumps' implementation trap is the other half of this decision: question ids are not safe to treat as globally shared, so the merge compares option sets, not ids. Reusing the bands is therefore a positive statement that these ARE the same question, not an accident.

design_decisions.change: site_variety is reweighted from 3 (near-inert at the two steps below) to 9 with new help text built on USHPA P4's concrete requirement, and a new question, xc_experience, is added at weight 8. NEITHER gates, and neither is a member of critical_check_floor.questions.
design_decisions.reason: knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 locates the sourced case for both ideas at this step and no earlier, and knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md calls this "the step in the ladder where both ideas are best evidenced". Site variety has the stronger case: two independent national bodies (USHPA P4's 5 flights at each of 5 sites, 3 inland; FFVL's Brevet de Pilote explicitly extending a pilot from 'known site only' to 'any site') treat it as a distinct, named milestone rather than a byproduct of hours. XC distance has a real but weaker case: BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating names specific distances (10/20/30km, a 10km declared goal, a 20km out-and-return), FFVL counts qualifying flights instead, and the two measure different things.
design_decisions.why_neither_gates: Three reasons, all recorded in the knowledge base. (1) knowledge/disagreements.md point 5: pilot-rating ladders and the EN wing-class ladder are different systems, and a pilot can hold P4 or Advanced Pilot while flying any class of wing. The step file's own caveat says these are reasonable as "supporting, non-gating signals at this step". (2) Joy Paragliding argues explicitly against tying wing upgrades to kilometres flown, on the grounds that adjacent-category performance differences are usually too small to matter and in-flight decisions affect an XC flight far more than the glider does. (3) The two best distance figures don't agree on what to measure, so any threshold would be picking a measurement system, not reading one off the sources.
design_decisions.how_the_wording_handles_the_counter-voic: xc_experience's help text states Joy Paragliding's argument in plain language, side by side with the rating-scheme figures, and says the question cannot hold the result on its own. That is deliberate: the question must not imply a kilometre bar the research does not support.

source.cites: "We think there's a real, sourced case for adding a site variety question from roughly the high-B→low-C step onward (two independent national bodies treat it as a distinct milestone, not just a function of hours)... We think the case for an XC distance question is weaker and more contested — real pilot-rating bodies use it, but a credible industry voice argues against its relevance to wing choice specifically, and the two best figures don't agree on what to count."
source.note: The weight difference (site_variety 9, xc_experience 8) encodes that relative confidence. Together they are 17 of 198 skills weight, 8.6% — enough to move a borderline pilot a band, not enough to hold a strong one back. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/07 is the persona that tests exactly that.

design_decisions.change: A new gate, 'collapse_response_entirely_untested', caps the result at Not yet for a pilot who has NEITHER practised collapses, wingovers and spirals (beyond theory) NOR ever handled a real collapse themselves. collapse_practice is also scored a full band harder than at the step below — self-practised tip folds drop from 0.6 to 0.45, which moves them below the Ready-blocker line.
design_decisions.reason: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#collapse-handling is explicit that the status of this skill changes here: "This is the first step where 'precise pilot input required for recovery' (the core EN-C certification language) starts being treated by sources as something a pilot needs to already be good at, rather than something to learn on the new wing." Three further voices point the same way from different directions: XC Mag's active-flying piece places EN-C in the more demanding part of a spectrum running from self-recovering intermediate wings to competition wings needing active input; USHPA P4 requires a demonstrated 50%-asymmetric-collapse recovery with directional control at roughly this level; and Simon Winkler argues that from about EN-C upward, wings resist collapsing so well that realistic training becomes hard to stage on the wing itself, so the muscle memory has to exist beforehand.
design_decisions.why_a_combination_and_not_a_single_answe: A single-answer gate on 'never practised' would cap a pilot who has caught and flown out a real half-wing collapse but never set one up deliberately — which is evidence of the skill, not absence of it. Requiring both halves to be empty means the gate fires only when there is no evidence from either direction. Equally important: SELF-practice clears the gate. A pilot who has pulled and released tip folds with height is blocked from Ready but not capped, so this is not an SIV gate by the back door — which would breach BRIEF.md and knowledge/disagreements.md point 1.

source.cites: Quoted above. Plus knowledge/disagreements.md point 12: Simon Winkler (expert, DHV instructor) argues that from roughly EN-C upward wings resist collapsing too strongly for an instructor to induce a representative collapse, so the training has to happen earlier on lower-class wings; Melchior Lindenstruth independently raises the practical version for EN-C two-liners.
source.note: This is the single most consequential new mechanism in this rubric and the clearest translation of the asymmetric-risk finding into behaviour. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/04 is the persona it exists for — a genuinely good, current, well-motivated XC pilot who has simply never worked on collapses, held at Not yet.

design_decisions.change: intended_flying_context is defined and used to select suggestions, but no exemption attaches to any Ready-blocker. thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.exemptions is deliberately empty, as at mid-B to high-B.
design_decisions.reason: Re-asked at this step rather than copied, and the answer comes out the same way with LESS argument than one rung down. At mid-B to high-B the decision was contested, because Hamerton offered roughly 100 hours of ridge soaring as an alternative route and the rubric had to decline it. Here no source offers any ridge-soaring equivalent at all: all three industry hours figures are thermic-hours figures, the step file says in terms that this is "the first point where sources explicitly expect a pilot to have flown (not just tolerated) genuinely turbulent thermic conditions, not just smooth-day XC", and the two pilot-rating ladders this step draws on add site variety and cross-country flying on top. There is no reading of this step's evidence that a soaring-only pilot clears, so there is nothing to exempt.
design_decisions.what_this_costs: A local-only pilot who answers 'I mostly soar rather than thermal' cannot reach Ready at this step however strong everything else is. They are told so in plain language by the 'local_plans_and_this_wings_purpose' suggestion and by the 'unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_control' rule message, rather than being silently blocked.

source.cites: "Consistent theme: this step marks the first point where sources explicitly expect a pilot to have flown (not just tolerated) genuinely turbulent thermic conditions, not just smooth-day XC."
source.note: The array is kept in the config, empty and annotated, so the structural difference from a-to-low-b.json and low-b-to-mid-b.json stays visible rather than looking like an omission. See thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.exemptions_deliberately_empty.

design_decisions.change: A new psychological question, 'effort_already_invested' (weight 9), asks what happens when a long drive or a long walk up meets a marginal day. At the three steps below, this material reaches the pilot only inside the 'peer_pressure_plan' suggestion.
design_decisions.reason: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#red-flags names the mechanism in this step's own file, attributes it to a named expert with relevant credentials and a survey behind him, and says in terms that it is "a concrete, nameable red flag the app could usefully ask about (e.g. 'would you still make this call if you hadn't already hiked/driven/waited to get here?')" — which is close to the wording used. The step file is honest that the pattern is general rather than specific to this boundary; it is promoted to a scored question here rather than at the steps below because this is the step whose own research names it, and because the flying this class is sold for (further from home, unfamiliar sites, planned XC) is exactly the flying that creates sunk costs.

source.cites: Bendicht Erb via Podz-Glidz Episode 35 (expert — flight instructor and certified sports psychologist, survey of 400+ pilots): pilots who have already invested significant effort to get airborne rationalise a launch in marginal conditions to avoid 'wasting' that effort, rather than assessing the conditions on their own merits.
source.note: Scored like the other decision-making questions rather than harder: a single expert voice on a general pattern supports a real weight, not a gate. It takes part in no gate. docs/design-context.md informs the framing — the question asks what the pilot DOES, not how they feel about it — and none of that document's terminology appears in the pilot-facing wording.

design_decisions.change: The manoeuvres-course bonus stays at a capped 2 points, byte-identical to all three steps below. The 'siv_before_you_upgrade' suggestion is priority 1 and has the broadest trigger of any SIV suggestion in the ladder, and the collapse-related gate and rule messages carry the timing argument in their own copy.
design_decisions.reason: This is the step where the pro-SIV material is strongest — Flybubble pairs SIV with its ~100-hour figure in one article and recommends it "especially" for C-curious pilots in another, and BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating actually requires a completed SIV course. But BRIEF.md says SIV "is optional context only and must not be a major factor, as its value is debated", and knowledge/disagreements.md point 1 adds the specific deflations: Hamerton's endorsement is not independent of Flybubble's (point 6, and the step file flags it at this step by name), BHPA's requirement attaches to a pilot rating rather than to an EN letter (point 5), and credible sources that take pilots to exactly this level — Daoust, USHPA's own syllabi, and a national competition series that requires P4 to enter — do not require SIV at all.
design_decisions.what_this_costs: A pilot who has done two SIV courses gains the same 2 points here as at A to low-B, which under-states how much several sources at this step think it matters. The compensation is that the suggestion sits at priority 1 and fires for a wide range of profiles, so almost every pilot short of this step sees it in their displayed set.

source.cites: Recommended handling: "SIV should be optional context only, never a hard gate, and should carry light weight at most, even at the D/2-liner/CCC steps where the pro-SIV sources are most emphatic... the safest design is as a small positive signal if completed, never a penalty or cap if not completed, and perhaps as a suggested next step in the 'things to work on' output for the C/D/2-liner steps specifically, where the evidence for its usefulness is strongest."
source.note: That last clause is an explicit instruction to do exactly what this rubric does: keep the points small and put the weight in the suggestion. knowledge/disagreements.md point 12 shapes the suggestion's content — it tells the pilot to train while they still own a wing a collapse can be induced on, rather than to book a course for later.

design_decisions.change: upgrade_motivation:want_more_performance scores 0.7 here against 0.75 at mid-B to high-B, and it is deliberately absent from the motive list in both combination gates. A separate suggestion, 'performance_chasing_reframe', fires only when that motive is paired with no evidence that the current wing has limited the pilot.
design_decisions.reason: A deliberate resolution of knowledge/disagreements.md point 9, which this step tests harder than any other. Passion Paragliding is "the most pointed source found anywhere in this knowledge base on this exact transition": its own view is that roughly half of pilots on EN-C wings shouldn't yet be on them, having upgraded chasing perceived performance rather than a demonstrated need, and it argues the within-class performance difference is usually very small, which makes performance-chasing a particularly weak reason AT THIS STEP. Yvonne Dathe corroborates from a credentialed sports-psychology angle. Set against that, Guschlbauer treats the wish to achieve goals as the force that drives real progression, Hamerton answers his own 'why upgrade?' question with 'to get more performance' without treating it as suspect, and Chrigel Maurer adds a third voice in the same camp by a different route — trained competence and a genuine fallback plan determine whether risk stays manageable, not the ambition of the plan.
design_decisions.what_this_costs_and_why_it_is_small: A one-notch markdown on one answer, which cannot gate anyone and cannot on its own drop a band. The diagnostic combination both camps agree on — an ambition-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere — is what the gates use, exactly as point 9 recommends.

source.cites: "Avoid treating 'wants more performance' or 'wants to fly with faster friends' alone as a hard penalty... The more diagnostic combination, supported by both camps, is an ambition-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere." Plus knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#psychological--mindset-factors for Passion Paragliding, Dathe and Maurer.
source.note: The German term Dathe uses for upgrading equipment to cover a skill gap is memorable and is deliberately never used in any pilot-facing copy, in this file or in the suggestions. Nothing pilot-facing claims a proportion of C pilots shouldn't be on their wings either — that is one author's own estimate, not a study, and repeating it as a statistic would overstate it.

design_decisions.change: 0.53 skills / 0.47 psychological, against 0.55/0.45 at A to low-B and mid-B to high-B and 0.52/0.48 at low-B to mid-B.
design_decisions.reason: Not a softening of the skills side — the skills evidence here is good. It reflects that the psychological material at this step is the strongest in the knowledge base for any boundary: Passion Paragliding writing specifically about this transition, two independently credentialed sports psychologists converging on treating hesitation as a protective signal (Dathe, and Theurillat via XC Mag), Chrigel Maurer on competence-and-fallback versus nominal ambition, the forum's finding that pilots disagree about which class actually feels calmer in bad air (which makes the pilot's own reported control in rough air a primary input rather than a supporting one), and the financial-asymmetry argument. BRIEF.md's requirement that psychological answers carry real weight is easier to satisfy honestly here than anywhere else.

source.cites: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note."
source.note: In practice the psychological half does even more than 0.47 suggests: response_when_rough is the highest-weighted question in the rubric, three of the twelve gates are driven partly by psychological answers, and the psychological Not yet floor is what stops strong hands buying out a poor answer set on motives, social pressure and unexplained incidents.

design_decisions.change: critical_check_floor.questions holds 10 questions, and four of them bite a band higher than at mid-B to high-B: collapse_practice (self-practice now fails), reading_the_day ('right about half the time' now fails), thermal_turn_control ('wide turns, losing the core' already failed, and 'not confident' drops to 0.0) and flying_frequency (monthly now scores 0.4 rather than 0.45).
design_decisions.reason: The list length is the same as one rung down; what changes is where the line falls on individual questions, and each move is individually sourced. collapse_practice: the skill changes status at this step from 'be practising' to 'be good at' (see the gate decision above). reading_the_day: Seb Ospina's reframe makes air-reading the defining readiness skill at this boundary rather than one skill among many — "only pilots who can already read and interpret that information benefit" — and USHPA P4 expects flights at unfamiliar sites in intermediate conditions, which is day-judgement away from home. This is the one bar mid-B to high-B deliberately declined to raise, and the reason to raise it here is specific rather than general. flying_frequency: both annual figures at this step (70 hours/year, and the ~50/year rule of thumb) are far above what monthly flying produces.
design_decisions.what_was_deliberately_left_out: site_variety and xc_experience (supporting signals only — see the XC decision above). ground_handling_kiting and ground_handling_practice (no source sets a bar at this step; knowledge/disagreements.md point 11 forbids inventing one). launch_reliability (this step's file says nothing about launches, so its gate rests on general accident data and a Ready-block would overreach — carried forward unchanged from mid-B to high-B). speed_bar (the one source specific to this step has uncertain provenance). Every cumulative-hours question. conditions_flown (no falsifiable marker exists — point 7).

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing starts transmitting genuinely useful extra information about the air, but only pilots who can already read and interpret that information benefit; pilots who can't will "notice a better glide and some more speed" and miss everything else. "This reframes readiness as an air-reading skill, not just an hours count."
source.note: ORDER MATTERS: the engine breaks on the first failing question, so the list is ordered most-to-least step-specific, with the two softest-sourced members (reading_the_day, reserve_familiarity) last. A reviewer changing the order should re-run tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/03 and /09.

design_decisions.change: incidents_12m:injury_or_reserve scores 0.0 on a weight-12 psychological question but fires no gate. Carried forward from config/scoring/a-to-low-b.json v2, low-b-to-mid-b.json v1 and mid-b-to-high-b.json v1 rather than re-litigated.
design_decisions.reason: An injury or reserve ride is not reliably about wing-class readiness — it can come from a bad landing or a ground-handling accident. The wing-class-relevant version of the same event, losing control after a collapse, is gated separately by 'collapse_control_lost', and the entirely-untested version is now gated by 'collapse_response_entirely_untested'.

source.cites: The brief's gate examples are capability signals ("frequent collapses they struggle to recover from, very low hours for the target class"), not incident outcomes.
source.note: The 'post_collapse_support' suggestion carries the weight for this answer, at priority 1.

owner_decisions: thresholds.ready.total_min is 78. It is synthesised, not sourced. It sits 2 above mid-B to high-B, 3 above low-B to mid-B and 6 above A to low-B, which encodes the asymmetric-risk finding rather than any figure from the research. The single most consequential number in this file after the thermic-hours scores.

Whether thermic_airtime should get its own 75-hour band at this step. We reused mid-B to high-B's bands so the question merges into one screen in a chained run, which leaves the 50-100 band straddling the 75-versus-100 disagreement and scored at 0.6. The honest alternative is bands of under_25 / 25_50 / 50_75 / 75_100 / over_100, at the cost of a second near-identical hours screen for any pilot running a mid-B to low-C chain. See meta.design_decisions 'v1-hours-bands-reused-from-the-step-below'.

Whether 'collapse_response_entirely_untested' should be a gate at all, or should stay a Ready-blocker as at the step below. It is the strongest new mechanism here and the clearest expression of the asymmetric-risk finding, but it caps a pilot who may be excellent in every other respect (tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/04). A reviewer could reasonably argue for demoting it. If it is demoted, the 'siv_before_you_upgrade' and 'collapse_practice_now' suggestions already carry the message.

Whether xc_experience should exist at this step at all. knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 is explicitly more doubtful about XC distance than about site variety, and Joy Paragliding argues against the whole idea. It is included at weight 8, non-gating and non-blocking, with its own counter-voice stated in its help text. The honest alternative is to drop it to weight 0 and keep it as a suggestion trigger only, which is what site_variety was at the two steps below.

Whether the manoeuvres-course bonus should rise above 2 points at this step. Several sources here are more emphatic about SIV than at any rung below, and BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating actually requires a course. We kept it at 2 because BRIEF.md is explicit and knowledge/disagreements.md point 1 deflates each of those sources individually. This is the place to change it if the owner disagrees — not the gates.

Whether 'doesnt_bother_me' on response_when_rough deserves its 0.5 (down from 0.55 at mid-B to high-B, 0.6 at the two steps below). It now sits exactly on the Ready-blocker line, so it passes by the narrowest possible margin. It rests on general extreme-sports literature plus the fact that this step's own sources treat genuinely turbulent thermic air as the working environment. Still a judgement, not a finding.

Whether the 'still_in_training' gate is worth keeping three rungs up the ladder. It is almost certainly inert. Kept because deferring to an instructor is the most conservative handling available and costs nothing.

max_rule_reasons_shown is 2 and max_gate_reasons_shown is 3, carried forward unchanged. With 12 gates and 10 Ready-blockers, a genuinely unready pilot can trip four or five at once; tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/06 trips four and is the one to read for whether the stacking reads as a telling-off.
meta.method: Each answer has a score from 0 to 1. Within a category, score = sum(weight x answer_score) / sum(weight of answered, scored questions) x 100. Total = 0.53 x skills + 0.47 x psychological, then bonuses are added and the total is clamped to 0-100. Gates are applied last and override the total.

weight_totals.note: Totals differ from the steps below (130/75 at A to low-B, 140/84 at low-B to mid-B, 164/84 at mid-B to high-B) because the question set differs — this step adds xc_experience and effort_already_invested and reweights site_variety. Only the within-category ratios matter; the category means are normalised.

source.cites: SAHPA's design pattern of defaulting an unregistered glider to the most demanding category unless a lower class is actively registered.
source.note: Applied here as: when the evidence is incomplete, default down rather than up. Carried forward unchanged from all three steps below.

meta.rounding: Round category and total scores to the nearest whole number for display only; compare thresholds against unrounded values.
meta.source_fields_are_internal: Every 'source' block in this file is provenance for the owner and reviewer only. Do not render 'ref', 'cites' or 'note' text in the UI. Pilot-facing copy in this file is exactly two things: the 'message' field on each gate, and the 'message' field on each entry under rule_messages.by_rule / rule_messages.fallback_by_rule_id. Everything else — including every 'purpose', 'note', 'reason', 'why_*', 'what_this_costs', 'what_was_deliberately_left_out' and 'disagreement_note' field — is internal. The rest of the pilot-facing copy lives in the questions and suggestions configs. docs/design-context.md informs several decisions here and is named in some source notes; it must never be named, quoted or paraphrased anywhere a pilot can see.

source.cites: The usable skills criteria at this boundary are substantial: a thermic-hours cluster (75-100+) from three industry sources, USHPA P4's official-adjacent proxy (250 flights, 75 hours airtime with 25+ thermic, demonstrated 50%-asymmetric recovery with directional control), BHPA Advanced Pilot's ~100 hours and specific XC distances, Seb Ospina's air-reading reframe, Simon Winkler on pitch sensitivity and the lightest touch, and the clearest speed-bar step-change anywhere in the ladder.
source.note: See meta.design_decisions 'v1-category-split-moves-closest-to-even-of-any-step'. The split is 0.53 not because the skills evidence is weak but because the psychological evidence at this step is unusually strong.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) is the most pointed source in the knowledge base on this exact transition, naming ego and peer pressure as drivers. Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz (expert, sports psychology) independently corroborates it and frames hesitation as a protective signal worth listening to. Chrigel Maurer via Podz-Glidz (expert) argues trained competence and a genuine fallback plan determine whether risk stays manageable, not the nominal ambition of the plan. The "High End Bs vs. Low EN Cs" forum thread shows pilots disagreeing about which class feels calmer in bad air, which the step file says "argues for the app weighting the pilot's own reported comfort/control in rough air fairly heavily at this step". Plus the resale/expensive-mistake asymmetry.
source.note: BRIEF.md: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note." Plus knowledge/disagreements.md point 9 for how motivation is scored without penalising ambition itself.

intended_flying_context.purpose: Named, reusable groupings of the 'ambitions' answer, used to decide which demands a pilot's own stated plans create. Never scored and never shown to the pilot. At this step they are referenced by suggestions only — see meta.design_decisions 'v1-no-stated-plans-exemption-at-this-step-either' for why no Ready-blocker exemption attaches to them here.

exposure_bound.label_internal: Plans that will put the pilot in thermic, mountain or high-workload air
exposure_bound.note: At this step these are the NORMAL plans for the class rather than stretching ones — the sources position low-C as a cross-country tier and the pilot-rating ladders this step borrows from expect demonstrated XC flying — so the profile tailors advice rather than adding scrutiny.

local_only.label_internal: Plans that stay inside local, ridge or coastal soaring
local_only.note: Requires a positive statement of local-only or no-particular-goal flying, not merely the absence of an ambition tick. A pilot who selects nothing at all is NOT local_only — no stated plans means no evidence of scope, and knowledge/disagreements.md point 5 says default down when evidence is missing. At this step the profile triggers an honest conversation suggestion rather than an exemption.

source.cites: Recommended handling: ambition must not be treated as a penalty in itself; the diagnostic combination is an ambition-flavoured motive paired with thin readiness elsewhere.
source.note: Using ambitions as scope context never costs the pilot a point. Structure carried forward from all three steps below so the four steps stay comparable, with the exemption deliberately absent here as at mid-B to high-B.

source.cites: BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating (official, extraction caveat) requires roughly 100 hours of airtime logged since the Pilot rating — the only figure at this step measured in general airtime rather than thermic airtime. USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) asks for 75 hours total airtime, of which 25+ must be thermal lift.
source.note: Weighted slightly higher than at mid-B to high-B (5), because here two pilot-rating ladders do give total-airtime figures, where at the step below every figure was thermic-only. Still well below thermic_airtime, because both of these are pilot-rating requirements rather than EN-letter ones (knowledge/disagreements.md point 5) and the industry sources that write about EN-C specifically all measure thermic hours.

total_airtime.disagreement_note: Bands reused byte-identically from mid-B to high-B so the question merges in a chained run; only the scores are harder. Full marks arrive at 200 hours even though the highest figure found is BHPA's ~100 since the Pilot rating, because that figure excludes everything flown before it. Nothing above 200 is distinguished, because no source distinguishes anything up there.

source.cites: USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) requires 250 total flights. The step file calls P4 "a reasonable official-adjacent proxy for 'ready for more demanding gear' at roughly this point in a pilot's development".
source.note: The first step in the ladder where any source gives a flight count anywhere near the boundary, which is why the weight rises from 3 to 5 — but it is a pilot-rating figure, so knowledge/disagreements.md point 5 keeps it small and non-gating.

total_flights.disagreement_note: The 150-300 band straddles P4's 250 figure, so a pilot at 180 flights and a pilot at 280 score identically. That is a real cost of reusing the step below's bands for merge safety, and it is accepted because the weight is 5 and the question gates and blocks nothing. See meta.owner_decisions.

source.cites: Flybubble's "Which Class?" (industry): roughly 100 cumulative hours of thermic flying plus some SIV experience for its "Sports (EN C)" tier. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry, same retailer, different article): 75+ hours of thermic flying for EN-C, flown regularly. 406 Paragliding (industry): 100+ hours of thermic flying specifically. The step file's consensus read: "cumulative-hours figures cluster loosely in the 75-100+ hour range across industry sources... No source gives a hard, well-corroborated single number — treat any figure here as a rough band, not a cutoff."
source.note: Highest single skills weight, and the only hours question that gates anything. The gates sit a long way below the figures — see 'thermic_hours_far_below_every_reading' — precisely because the sources don't agree with each other and one of them disagrees with itself.

thermic_airtime.disagreement_note: The 50-100 band contains BOTH published readings (75 and 100) and scores 0.6: above the Ready-blocker line, well short of full marks. That is the honest value for a band the evidence cannot resolve — a pilot in it may be below both figures or above the lower one, and nothing in the sources lets the rubric tell. 25-50 scores 0.3 against 0.6 at mid-B to high-B, because the figure it is being measured against has risen from roughly 50 to 75-100. Full marks arrive at the upper reading and nothing is gained above it. knowledge/disagreements.md point 2 is why this is scored in bands and not against a single number; point 6 is why Flybubble's internal inconsistency is treated as a genuine range rather than resolved in either direction.

source.cites: paraglidingforum.com (community, used only to show rough practitioner consensus): a commonly repeated rule of thumb of roughly 50+ flying hours per year before considering EN-C, "alongside the more important qualitative test of feeling in control in rough air, not just calm air". Passion Paragliding (industry): 70 hours/year before EN-C. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" adds the qualifier "flown regularly" to its 75-hour figure.
source.note: knowledge/disagreements.md point 2 requires currency to be weighted independently of the lifetime total. Weighted equal to flying_frequency and above total_airtime, because both numeric figures at this step are annual rather than cumulative — the opposite emphasis from the industry articles, and worth taking seriously as a second, independent framing.

airtime_last_12m.disagreement_note: The 50-80 band contains both annual figures (50 and 70) and scores 0.9 rather than 1.0, so the conservative reading of the pair sits just below full marks rather than at the top of the scale. knowledge/disagreements.md point 10 flags Passion Paragliding's 70 as uncorroborated and the forum figure is explicitly not a citable criterion, so neither is used as a bar to clear — they shape the scale, not the threshold. Bands reused byte-identically from mid-B to high-B for merge safety.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) argues that upgrading without a demonstrated need is the characteristic error at this step specifically. Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert) frames readiness as being able to use what a better wing tells you, which presupposes having used up what the current one tells you.
source.note: No source gives a figure for hours-on-a-high-B before a low-C, so this is scored as evidence of having used the current wing rather than against a threshold. The behavioural version of the same idea is asked directly by wing_limiting_evidence, which carries more weight. Bands reused byte-identically from the two steps below.

current_wing_time.disagreement_note: Scored harder than at mid-B to high-B (0.2/0.45/0.8/1.0) on the strength of the asymmetric-risk finding, not on a figure — there isn't one. knowledge/disagreements.md point 10 records a community rule of thumb of 150-200 hours per wing-class step, which would be stricter again; it is treated as indicative colour only, exactly as point 10 instructs.

source.cites: USHPA's syllabus defers wing choice to whatever the manufacturer recommends rather than naming an EN letter, i.e. the call sits with the school or instructor while a pilot is still under supervision.
source.note: Phrased as training status, never as a national rating, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 5. Almost certainly inert three rungs up the ladder — see meta.owner_decisions.

source.cites: paraglidingforum.com (community): the commonly repeated rule of thumb is roughly 50+ hours per year — i.e. current, regular flying — before considering EN-C. Passion Paragliding (industry): 70 hours/year. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry): 75+ hours of thermic flying, "flown regularly".
source.note: Weighted equal to airtime_last_12m: one measures how much, the other how recently and how evenly spread. Together they drive the 'occasional_pilot_profile' gate, which is widened at this step relative to mid-B to high-B.

flying_frequency.disagreement_note: 'About once a month' scores 0.4 here against 0.45 at mid-B to high-B and 0.55/0.5 at the two steps below — a second one-band tightening on the same answer. Monthly flying produces nowhere near 50 or 70 hours a year, which are the two figures this step actually has. No source gives a frequency figure, so this blocks Ready rather than gating on its own; the gate needs a thin 12-month total alongside it.

source.cites: "Ground handling (added Oct 2026): no source ties a specific ground-handling test to this exact boundary. Fly With Greg's ground-handling progression (expert) is the most relevant general material available — its more advanced exercises (stall-point recognition, depowering, strong-wind launch control) match the kind of active-piloting fluency this step's sources already expect in the air, but no source explicitly states 'you should be able to do X on the ground before flying a low-C.'"
source.note: Scored, never gated, and not a Ready-blocker — identical treatment to both steps below. knowledge/disagreements.md point 11 is why it is asked at all: the one piece of official accident data touching on this found accident rates essentially equivalent across P1-P4 ratings with launch and ground-phase problems a persistent contributor, and Urs Aschmann frames kiting as a lifelong skill with real headroom past the beginner stage.

ground_handling_kiting.disagreement_note: Option set reused byte-identically from mid-B to high-B, where it was extended upward with Aschmann's named advanced drills. Scores are a notch harder here but full marks remain genuinely optional: a pilot can reach Ready at 0.8. The scale's top is a reading of Aschmann's and Greg's progressions rather than a bar any source sets at this boundary.

source.cites: Urs Aschmann via Podz-Glidz Episode 37 (expert, ground-handling specialist) treats ground handling as never finished, with named exercises that only make sense well past the beginner stage; USHPA's 2001 accident data gives the official-side reason not to assume it is solved by this point.
source.note: Low weight — a habit question, used mainly to trigger suggestions. Never gates, never blocks.

source.cites: USHPA's 2001 Paragliding Accident Summary (official): around 64% of accidents occurred on the ground or immediately after launch, and accident rates were essentially equivalent across P1-P4 pilot ratings. Greg Hamerton via FAI/CIVL safety pages (expert) notes risk rises from unfamiliarity after any gear change, which lands on launches first.
source.note: Honest flag, carried forward from mid-B to high-B: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md says nothing about launching either. This question rests on general accident data, not on a step-specific criterion, which is why it keeps its weight and its gate on the worst band but is NOT a Ready-blocker. USHPA P4's requirement of 5 flights at each of 5 different sites is the nearest thing to a launch-breadth criterion at this step, and it is scored through site_variety rather than here.

launch_reliability.disagreement_note: Full marks require reliability across a range of conditions, which is consistent with P4's site-variety expectation but is not a launch standard any source states for this boundary.

source.cites: All three industry hours figures measure thermic flying (Flybubble 100, Flybubble 75, 406 Paragliding 100+), which makes competent thermalling the defining activity of this step. USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) adds at least three one-hour thermal-lift flights from at least two different sites. Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert) supplies the quality bar: the wing's extra information is only useful to a pilot who can already read it.
source.note: Question reused byte-identically from the two steps below; only the scores are harder.

thermal_turn_control.disagreement_note: Non-monotonic. 'I mostly soar or glide rather than thermal' stays at 0.5 — neutral and low-information rather than a failure, exactly as at all three steps below. The pilot has not done something badly, they have not done it. It blocks Ready through thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks, with NO stated-plans exemption, as at mid-B to high-B. 'I can centre a climb and change bank deliberately' drops from 0.8 to 0.75, because at 75-100 thermic hours that is the expected standard rather than an achievement.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing starts transmitting genuinely useful extra information about the air, but "only pilots who can already read and interpret that information benefit; pilots who can't will 'notice a better glide and some more speed' and miss everything else the wing is telling them. This reframes readiness as an air-reading skill, not just an hours count." USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) expects 5 flights at each of 5 different sites in Intermediate-level conditions, 3 of them inland — judgement away from home.
source.note: Weight rises from 9 to 11 and the bar rises a band, which is the one place this rubric raises a check that mid-B to high-B deliberately declined to raise. The reason is specific rather than general: Ospina's reframe makes air-reading THE readiness question at this boundary, and it is the only skills criterion at this step with that status.

reading_the_day.disagreement_note: 'Right about half the time' drops from 0.5 (exactly on the Ready-blocker line at both steps below) to 0.45 (just under it). This is a deliberate one-notch move and the honest caveat is that no source gives an accuracy standard for reading a day at this step either — what has changed is that a named industry/expert source now makes air-reading the defining skill rather than one of several. A reviewer who thinks that is too fine a distinction should put it back to 0.5; tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/05 is the persona affected.

source.cites: Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor) describes EN-C wings as having pitch sensitivity demanding "the lightest touch". XC Mag's active-flying piece (industry) describes a spectrum from school wings (stable through major collapses) through intermediate wings (self-recovering) to competition-style wings needing active pilot input, and places EN-C in the more demanding part of it — consistent with the EN-C certification language about precise pilot input.
source.note: Joint-highest skills weight with thermic_airtime's 15 above it. Of everything in this questionnaire this is the closest read on whether the pilot's existing habits already cover what a less damped, more pitch-sensitive wing will ask for.

active_piloting.disagreement_note: 'I work the brakes to keep the pressure even and the wing overhead' scores 0.6 here, 0.7 at mid-B to high-B and 0.9 at low-B to mid-B. It still passes the Ready-blocker comfortably at all three. The reason it keeps falling is Winkler's description, which gets more specific the higher the class: phase-dependent hands at high-B, and "the lightest touch" on a pitch-sensitive C. Working the brakes evenly is good flying that is one notch below what this step's own source describes, which is what 0.6 encodes.

source.cites: "Consistent theme: this step marks the first point where sources explicitly expect a pilot to have flown (not just tolerated) genuinely turbulent thermic conditions, not just smooth-day XC."
source.note: Scored as a description of exposure, monotonic to the top. The same step file records, from an owner-prompted gap-check, that even here no source frames this as a specific, falsifiable 'strongest conditions survived without a collapse' marker — it stays qualitative throughout — so no such question exists in this rubric.

conditions_flown.disagreement_note: The top band takes full marks and 'proper thermic days, fairly regularly' drops from 1.0 at mid-B to high-B to 0.9 here. That is the only place in this rubric where a previously-perfect answer is marked down, and the reason is the word 'genuinely turbulent' in the source above: at this step the sources ask for turbulent thermic air specifically, not just regular thermic air. knowledge/disagreements.md point 7 is why there is no collapse-free-survival question.

source.cites: USHPA's P4 (Advanced) syllabus (official via AirAddict) requires 5 flights at each of 5 different sites in Intermediate-level conditions (3 of them inland), plus at least three 1-hour thermal-lift flights originating from at least 2 different sites, plus having flown a minimum of 5 different canopies — "the single clearest, most concrete official site-variety requirement found anywhere in this research". FFVL's Brevet de Pilote (official) independently extends a pilot from "known site only" to "any site", framed by Soaring Académie as deliberately "discovering new sites and varying flight conditions". The step file: "Two independent national associations treating site/terrain variety as a distinct, named milestone — not just a byproduct of more hours — is a genuinely useful, well-corroborated finding for this step."
source.note: Weight rises from 3 (near-inert at the two steps below, carried forward only to avoid a question appearing, vanishing and reappearing) to 9 here, which is where knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 locates the sourced case. Never gates and is NOT a Ready-blocker, per point 5's caution that pilot-rating ladders are a separate system from the EN ladder.

site_variety.disagreement_note: The floor drops from 0.4 at the two steps below to 0.2, because here the question has real evidence behind it rather than being a placeholder. Option set reused byte-identically for merge safety, which means the options describe variety qualitatively where P4 counts it numerically — a deliberate choice, since importing '5 flights at each of 5 sites' into the option labels would present a pilot-rating requirement as a wing-class one.

source.cites: BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating (official, extraction caveat) requires individual flights over 10km, 20km and 30km, a declared-goal flight over 10km, and a 20km out-and-return, alongside roughly 100 hours since the Pilot rating — "the clearest instance anywhere in this research of a credible body tying progression explicitly to specific XC distances flown". FFVL's Brevet de Pilote Confirmé (official, search-summary level only) instead requires a count of qualifying distance flights, circa 10. The counter-voice: Joy Paragliding (industry) argues there is "no universal answer tied to hours or kilometers" for wing upgrades and that adjacent-category glide differences are often too small to matter.
source.note: New question, and it exists at this step only. The option bands deliberately blend both measurement systems — the middle bands describe a COUNT of shortish flights (FFVL's framing) and the top bands describe single-flight DISTANCE and declared tasks (BHPA's framing) — because knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 records that the two best figures disagree about what to measure and the app has to either pick or avoid committing. This avoids committing.

xc_experience.disagreement_note: Never gates and is NOT a Ready-blocker, and the floor is 0.2 rather than 0, both because of Joy Paragliding's argument and because every figure behind this question is a pilot-rating requirement rather than an EN-letter one (knowledge/disagreements.md point 5). The pilot-facing help text states that counter-argument explicitly, so the question cannot read as a kilometre bar. Flybubble's XC Secrets article (industry) pushes the same way from a different angle — it recommends flying a wing one class below what you think you can handle, and says the hundreds of decisions in a cross-country flight each matter more to the outcome than a wing upgrade.

source.cites: "Speed bar (added Oct 2026): this is the step where sources describe the clearest behavioural step-change in bar use. A class-by-class speedbar ladder mirrored on GitHub (provenance uncertain, see sources.md) states that by EN-C a pilot should expect to glide on half bar routinely, unless in lift or tailwind — a step up from the occasional, between-thermal use expected on EN-B." Flybubble's Speed To Fly Basics (industry), via knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md: higher-performance categories reward bar use at lower headwind and sink thresholds. XC Mag's speed bar tips (industry): easing onto the bar while watching pitch reaches full speed with meaningfully more height in hand than stomping it on.
source.note: Weight rises from 6 to 8 because this is the step with the clearest described behavioural change — but NOT a Ready-blocker, because the one source specific to this boundary has uncertain provenance. That asymmetry is deliberate and is recorded in gates_deliberately_not_included.

speed_bar.disagreement_note: Non-monotonic, and the shape has moved up again: 'a bit of bar on most glides' is full marks' worth of behaviour at A to low-B, 0.9 at mid-B to high-B and 0.8 here, because the EN-C description is routine half bar rather than occasional bar. 'Stomp it on' scores level with never having tried, on the strength of XC Mag's height-in-hand contrast and Daoust's warning that stomping the bar makes a collapse more likely — which matters more on a wing whose certification language assumes precise input to recover.

source.cites: "This is the first step where 'precise pilot input required for recovery' (the core EN-C certification language) starts being treated by sources as something a pilot needs to already be good at, rather than something to learn on the new wing." USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) requires a demonstrated 50%-asymmetric-collapse recovery with directional control, which is what the 'around half the wing, and I caught it and flew it out' band describes.
source.note: Together with collapse_practice this question drives the new 'collapse_response_entirely_untested' gate. P4's 'with directional control' qualifier is handled in the suggestions rather than by splitting the option, because asking a pilot to self-report whether they held a heading during a collapse would get an unreliable answer.

collapse_experience.disagreement_note: Non-monotonic. 'Never' sits at exactly 0.5 — on the Ready-blocker line, so it passes by the narrowest margin — against 0.55 at mid-B to high-B and 0.6 at the steps below. The reasoning is that 75-100 hours of thermic flying with no collapse at all is less informative than the same answer from a low-B soaring pilot, not that the absence of an event is a fault: no source treats having had a collapse as a prerequisite, and a pilot must never be dropped a band for it. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/02 reaches Ready with this answer, which is the guard against drift. The two worst answers fire the 'collapse_control_lost' gate; 'I froze' blocks Ready, and combines into the new gate if there has also been no practice.

source.cites: The EN-C certification language (precise pilot input required for recovery) treated by this step's sources as a skill to arrive with. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry) recommends ongoing wingover, spiral and asymmetric practice alongside an SIV course for C-curious pilots. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor): realistic collapse training becomes much harder to simulate once a pilot is already on a C-class wing, "reinforcing that the collapse-recovery skill this step's sources expect should ideally already be well-practised from training on earlier, lower-class gear, not something to pick up on the C-wing itself."
source.note: Scored a full band harder than at mid-B to high-B, remains a Ready-blocker, and is now one half of a gate. See meta.design_decisions 'v1-collapse-response-gets-a-gate-of-its-own'. Option set reused byte-identically from the step below.

collapse_practice.disagreement_note: Self-practised tip folds drop from 0.6 at mid-B to high-B to 0.45, which moves them below the Ready-blocker line — the single most consequential scoring change in this rubric. The justification is the status change recorded in the source above: one rung down, regular practice is what a source asks you to be DOING; here, precise recovery is what the class assumes you can already DO. Note what still does not happen: self-practice CLEARS the new gate, so a pilot who has worked on tip folds alone is held at Nearly ready, never capped. Full marks still require a course, which is why the bonus for having done one is separate and tiny — this question must not become an SIV requirement by the back door.

source.cites: Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry) names spirals specifically among the manoeuvres to be practising, alongside wingovers and asymmetrics, for pilots at and around this step.
source.note: Separate from collapse_practice because having a way down is about options under pressure rather than about recovery, and because a pilot flying the cross-country distances this step's rating ladders expect is further from home when they need one.

source.cites: USHPA P2 (official) includes reserve-deployment and PLF knowledge among its required skills.
source.note: Cross-referenced from three steps below and flagged as such: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md names no reserve criterion either. Carried forward, and kept as a Ready-blocker, on knowledge/disagreements.md point 5's conservative default and because not being sure you could find the handle is cheap to fix and bad at any step. This remains the weakest-sourced member of critical_check_floor.questions, exactly as recorded at the two steps below, and sits last in that list for that reason.

reserve_familiarity.disagreement_note: 'I know where the handle is but have never practised' is held at exactly 0.5 rather than dropped below the line, unlike four other questions at this step. Deliberate: there is no step-specific source to justify tightening it, and tightening an unsourced check is exactly the move knowledge/disagreements.md point 11 warns against in the ground-handling context.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) states as its own view that roughly half of pilots flying EN-C wings shouldn't yet be on them, having upgraded chasing perceived performance rather than a demonstrated need, and that for most B/C pilots the performance difference within a class is "usually very small", making performance-chasing a particularly weak reason at this specific step. Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert), via knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md: real readiness looks like having already been limited by the current wing in practice. Joy Paragliding (industry) and Flybubble's XC Secrets (industry) both argue the adjacent-category performance difference is usually too small to be the thing holding a pilot back.
source.note: Categorised as skills rather than psychological on purpose: it asks for evidence from flights flown, not for a motive. The motive lives in upgrade_motivation. The diagnostic pairing of the two is what the 'aspirational_rather_than_demonstrated' gate uses, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 9.

wing_limiting_evidence.disagreement_note: 'Left behind on glides' scores 0.75 rather than full marks, slightly below mid-B to high-B's 0.8, because two separate industry sources argue at this step specifically that the glide difference between adjacent categories is usually too small to explain being left behind — so that answer may be describing a climb-rate, route-choice or decision-making gap rather than a wing gap. It is still strong evidence of having felt a limit, which is why it is well above the middle.

source.cites: USHPA's syllabus defers the wing-class decision to the manufacturer's recommendation rather than to an EN letter, and in practice to the instructor applying it; BRIEF.md requires the app to recommend discussing the upgrade with an instructor regardless of result.
source.note: Someone who has watched this pilot fly is better evidence than anything in this questionnaire, and it matters particularly here: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md records Greg Hamerton being explicit that the certification letter alone doesn't tell a pilot how often a given wing actually collapses, so somebody who knows both the pilot and the specific wing is doing work no form can do. A direct 'wait' is a gate.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) names ego ("to validate your identity as a real pilot") and peer pressure explicitly as drivers at this transition, and argues performance-chasing is a particularly weak reason here because the within-class difference is usually very small. Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz Episode 109 (expert, sports psychology) independently corroborates from a credentialed angle, naming upgrading equipment to compensate for a skill gap rather than closing it. The counterweights: Guschlbauer via XC Mag's 'The Head Game' treats the wish to achieve goals as the necessary force behind progression, Hamerton answers his own 'why upgrade?' with 'to get more performance' without treating it as suspect, and Chrigel Maurer via Podz-Glidz Episode 114 argues trained competence and a genuine fallback plan determine whether risk stays manageable, not the ambition of the plan.
source.note: Conservative resolution of knowledge/disagreements.md point 9 — see meta.design_decisions 'v1-performance-chasing-is-marked-down-but-never-gated'. 'I want more glide and speed' is marked down one notch to 0.7 but takes part in no gate.

upgrade_motivation.disagreement_note: Two changes from mid-B to high-B, both small and both sourced to this step. 'I want more glide and speed' drops 0.75 to 0.7, on Passion Paragliding's argument that the within-class performance difference is usually very small here. 'I need a new wing anyway so I may as well go up' drops 0.5 to 0.4, on the resale asymmetry recorded in this step's file — a C bought on that reasoning is the expensive mistake the community warns about, where the equivalent B purchase rarely is. 'Hoping a better wing will cope with conditions I find hard' is 0.0, the only zero in the rubric's motivation question, because at this boundary it is not merely optimistic but backwards.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing starts transmitting genuinely useful extra information about the air. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor): EN-C wings have pitch sensitivity demanding "the lightest touch". The EN-C certification language: precise pilot input required for recovery. Nova (manufacturer): frames its own entry-level C as "a small step" for pilots already comfortable on its benchmark high-B.
source.note: The accurate expectation at this boundary is more information, a lighter touch and precise input if it folds — which is why that answer is the only one taking full marks. The question text names the target class, which is why this is one of only three questions at this step that does NOT merge with mid-B to high-B.

wing_expectation.disagreement_note: 'A bit more glide and speed — not a huge difference' scores 0.85, slightly BELOW mid-B to high-B's 0.9, and the reasoning is finely balanced. In favour of scoring it high: Nova markets its entry C as a small step from its benchmark high-B, Joy Paragliding and Flybubble both argue adjacent-category performance differences are small, and knowledge/disagreements.md point 3 names this boundary as the fuzziest on the ladder — so a pilot who says 'not a huge difference' is agreeing with several credible sources about PERFORMANCE. Against: the recovery-behaviour difference is real and is the thing this step's own sources care about, so the answer under-reads the part that matters. The deduction is deliberately small, and it is the reason the 'expectation_research' suggestion fires on this answer rather than any gate.

source.cites: Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz (expert, psychology graduate with formal sports-psychology training) favours process-oriented goals over outcome-oriented ones, based on her own coaching caseload. Guschlbauer via XC Mag's 'The Head Game' (industry/expert) treats "the wish to achieve certain goals" as the necessary force behind real progression.
source.note: Resolved toward point 9's recommended handling: chasing distance is not penalised hard, only comparison with peers is.

progress_goals.disagreement_note: 'Flying further and getting my distances up' scores 0.7, the most generous value for that answer anywhere in the ladder (0.6 at low-B to mid-B, 0.65 at mid-B to high-B). This is the step where two official rating ladders actually require demonstrated distance flying, so a distance goal is better matched to the class here than anywhere below. 'Keeping ahead of peers' drops from 0.2 to 0.15, because this is the step where a named industry source identifies peer comparison as the characteristic error.

source.cites: Greg Hamerton via FAI/CIVL's safety pages (expert): risk rises from unfamiliarity after any gear change, so deliberately compensate elsewhere for a period — more conservative sites, flying less aggressively, front-loaded study of the new wing's specific handling. The same source is explicit that the EN letter on its own is only a guideline and doesn't tell a pilot how often a given wing actually collapses, which is an argument for treating any specific new wing as unknown until flown.
source.note: Scored harder than at mid-B to high-B (0.2 and 0.05 for the two dismissive answers, against 0.25 and 0.1), on the asymmetric-risk finding plus Winkler's point that this is the class where realistic collapse practice stops being available — so the transition period has less margin for learning on the job.

source.cites: Recommended handling: avoid treating "wants more performance" or "wants to fly with faster friends" alone as a penalty; the diagnostic combination is an ambition-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere.
source.note: Deliberately zero-weighted — no answer here adds or removes a single point. At this step ambitions affect the result in exactly one scoring place: the 'ambition_without_readiness' combination gate. As at mid-B to high-B they exempt nothing, so the only direction they can move a result is the conservative one. Otherwise they only shape which suggestions appear. Reinforced at this step by Chrigel Maurer (expert), who argues the nominal ambition of a plan is not what determines whether its risk stays manageable.

source.cites: "The community thread on 'High End Bs vs. Low EN Cs' shows pilots disagreeing about which actually feels calmer in bad air — some find a well-behaved low-C more reassuring in strong turbulence than a twitchy high-B. This argues for the app weighting the pilot's own reported comfort/control in rough air fairly heavily at this step, rather than leaning only on the EN letter." paraglidingforum.com (community) pairs its annual-hours rule of thumb with "the more important qualitative test of feeling in control in rough air, not just calm air".
source.note: Highest single weight in the whole rubric, skills or psychological, and it is the one place the step file explicitly tells the app to weight something heavily. It asks what the pilot does under load rather than whether they feel nervous: nerves are not scored down, and 'heart rate goes up, but I carry on flying the wing' scores 0.75. Required by docs/design-context.md, whose terminology appears nowhere pilot-facing.

response_when_rough.disagreement_note: 'It doesn't really bother me' sits at exactly 0.5 — on the Ready-blocker line, passing by the narrowest margin — against 0.55 at mid-B to high-B and 0.6 at the two steps below. It rests on general extreme-sports literature in knowledge/sources.md associating risk-seeking and low threat-appraisal with higher injury rates, plus the fact that this step's own sources treat genuinely turbulent thermic air as the working environment and its own psychologists treat hesitation as useful information. That literature is not paragliding-specific, so this stays a judgement — flagged in meta.owner_decisions.

source.cites: Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz Episode 109 (expert, sports psychologist) frames fear or hesitation before a flight as a protective signal worth listening to rather than overriding, and offers a reframe for a pilot who hesitates at this step specifically: choosing not to fly, or not to upgrade yet, when honest self-assessed skill doesn't match the conditions or the wing, is sound judgement rather than something to feel embarrassed about. The step file records her as converging independently with Thomas Theurillat via XC Mag's 'The Head Game'.
source.note: Scoring 'yes, and I was happy with the call' at full marks is the clearest place this rubric refuses to reward pressing on. Required by docs/design-context.md's safety guard, which forbids any question or score that nudges an accurately hesitant pilot toward upgrading.

decline_to_fly.disagreement_note: 'It hasn't come up' scores 0.45, down from 0.5 at mid-B to high-B and 0.55 at the two steps below. At a step whose own sources describe regular thermic and cross-country flying from varied sites, never having turned down a day in several months is less likely to mean the question genuinely has not arisen. Still well clear of the 0.15 given to 'I generally launch and see how it goes', because an absence of occasions is not the same as a habit of pressing on.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) names peer pressure explicitly as one of the two unhealthy upgrade drivers at this transition, alongside ego. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV), via knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md, names social pressure plainly as a driver of unnecessary risk-taking.
source.note: Asks about behaviour under social pressure rather than about self-image, which is why it is scored more firmly than the motivation question itself. Sits alongside the new effort_already_invested question: one is pressure from other people, the other is pressure from your own sunk effort, and they are different failure modes.

source.cites: Bendicht Erb via Podz-Glidz Episode 35 (expert — flight instructor and certified sports psychologist, survey of 400+ pilots): pilots who have already invested significant effort to get airborne (e.g. a long hike-and-fly approach) rationalise a launch in marginal conditions to avoid "wasting" that effort, rather than assessing the conditions on their own merits. The step file names this "a concrete, nameable red flag the app could usefully ask about" and supplies the question's shape.
source.note: New question at this step. The step file is honest that the pattern is general rather than specific to this boundary, which is why it is weighted like the other decision-making questions rather than harder, and why it takes part in no gate. Supported indirectly by Chrigel Maurer (expert), whose point is that what keeps risk manageable is trained competence and a genuine fallback plan — and 'I've already driven three hours' is the opposite of a fallback plan.

effort_already_invested.disagreement_note: 'I feel it pulling at me, but I'll usually wait it out' scores 0.7 rather than near-full, deliberately: Erb's point is that recognising the pull is the mechanism working on you, so an honest 'I feel it' is good self-knowledge but not the same as the journey genuinely not entering the decision. 'Hasn't come up — my flying is mostly close to home' scores 0.55, neutral and low-information, exactly like the other 'not come up' answers in this rubric — it must not be read as a fault, and it must not score as evidence either.

source.cites: "Honesty about recent incidents and near misses" is listed as a required psychological input.
source.note: Non-monotonic: an honest, reflected-on near miss scores higher (1.0) than 'nothing happened' (0.85), because the first gives evidence of a working debrief habit and the second gives no evidence either way. Supported by Bendicht Erb via Podz-Glidz (expert) on structured incident processing and by Dathe's staged re-exposure approach. No standalone gate; see meta.design_decisions 'v1-no-standalone-incident-gate'.

source.cites: Recommended handling: SIV should be optional context only, never a hard gate, and should carry light weight at most — a small positive signal if completed, never a penalty or cap if not. "Perhaps as a suggested next step in the 'things to work on' output for the C/D/2-liner steps specifically, where the evidence for its usefulness is strongest."
source.note: Byte-identical to all three steps below, deliberately, even though this is the first step where several source types recommend SIV and one official pilot rating (BHPA Advanced Pilot) actually requires a course. BRIEF.md is explicit that SIV must not be a major factor. The whole of this step's extra emphasis sits in the priority-1 'siv_before_you_upgrade' suggestion and in the collapse gate and rule messages. Flagged in meta.owner_decisions as the single place to change if the owner disagrees — raising the bonus is a far safer change than adding a gate.

source.cites: The forum consensus recorded in the step file: "the penalty for choosing a C when you should be on a B can be rather more severe than the penalty for flying a B when you should have gone for a C" — i.e., sources agree err on the side of caution at this specific boundary more than at earlier ones. Plus knowledge/disagreements.md point 5's conservative-by-default pattern.
source.note: 78 against 76 at mid-B to high-B, 75 at low-B to mid-B and 72 at A to low-B. The Nearly ready band is 23 points wide (55 to 78). Category floors rise with it (72/68 against 70/65 one rung down) so neither half can stand in for the other at a more demanding class. All of these are synthesised figures, not sourced ones — see meta.owner_decisions.

source.cites: Each member is sourced at this boundary: thermic_airtime (the 75-100+ cluster, three industry articles); collapse_practice and collapse_experience (the EN-C 'precise pilot input required' language treated as a skill to arrive with, plus Flybubble's ongoing-practice recommendation, plus USHPA P4's demonstrated asymmetric recovery, plus Winkler's training-feasibility argument); wing_limiting_evidence (Passion Paragliding on upgrading without demonstrated need, Ospina on earned readiness); active_piloting (Winkler on pitch sensitivity and the lightest touch, XC Mag placing EN-C in the demanding part of the active-flying spectrum); thermal_turn_control (thermic flying is the activity every hours figure measures, plus P4's thermal-lift flights); response_when_rough (the step file's explicit instruction to weight reported control in rough air heavily here); flying_frequency (both annual figures, 50 and 70 hours/year); reading_the_day (Ospina's air-reading reframe, plus P4's unfamiliar-site expectation).
source.note: ORDER MATTERS: the engine breaks on the first failing question, so WHICH message a pilot sees depends on the order, and the list is ordered most-to-least step-specific. thermic_airtime is first because it is the number the pilot most needs to hear named; collapse_practice is second because it is the check whose status actually changes at this boundary. reading_the_day and reserve_familiarity are last — reading_the_day because its tightening rests on one source's reframe rather than on a stated standard, reserve_familiarity because it is borrowed from USHPA P2 three rungs down. Deliberately EXCLUDED, each for a recorded reason: site_variety and xc_experience (supporting signals only, per knowledge/disagreements.md points 5 and 14); ground_handling_kiting and ground_handling_practice (no bar exists at this step — point 11); launch_reliability (this step's file says nothing about launches); speed_bar (the one step-specific source has uncertain provenance); conditions_flown (no falsifiable marker — point 7); and every cumulative-hours question.

source.cites: SAHPA's pattern of defaulting to the most conservative category unless a lower one is actively evidenced.
