source.note: All three industry hours figures for this step measure thermic flying, and the step file says this is the first point where sources explicitly expect genuinely turbulent thermic conditions to have been flown rather than tolerated. A pilot who does not thermal therefore has no evidence either way about the main activity the class is positioned for. Treated as not-yet-demonstrated rather than as a failure: it scores 0.5 (neutral), fires no gate, and passes the critical_check_floor. Only one answer is listed, deliberately — xc_experience:none and site_variety:home_site_only are NOT here, because knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 makes them supporting signals rather than checks, and blocking Ready on them would be gating on pilot-rating criteria by another name.

exemptions_deliberately_empty.what_this_differs_from: config/scoring/a-to-low-b.json has 'stated_plans_dont_require_rough_air_judgement' and config/scoring/low-b-to-mid-b.json has 'stated_plans_dont_require_thermal_evidence'. Both let a pilot whose stated plans are local, ridge or coastal soaring reach Ready with an untested thermalling answer. config/scoring/mid-b-to-high-b.json removed it. There is no equivalent here either, and that is a deliberate decision rather than an omission or a copy-paste.
exemptions_deliberately_empty.reason: Re-decided at this step rather than inherited, and the answer is the same with less argument than one rung down. At mid-B to high-B the call was genuinely contested, because Hamerton offered roughly 100 hours of ridge soaring as an alternative qualifying route and the rubric had to decline it. Here no source offers any ridge equivalent at all: all three industry hours figures are thermic-hours figures, the step file calls this the first point where genuinely turbulent thermic flying is explicitly expected, and the two pilot-rating ladders this step borrows from add cross-country flying and site variety on top of that. There is no reading of this step's evidence that a soaring-only pilot clears, so there is nothing to exempt.
exemptions_deliberately_empty.how_the_pilot_is_told: The 'local_plans_and_this_wings_purpose' suggestion fires for exactly the profile that would have been exempted (local-only plans plus a smooth or ridge conditions answer) and explains in plain language what a low-C would and would not give them, ending with alternatives rather than a warning. The 'unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_control' rule message says the same thing in the result itself. The block is explained, never silent.

source.cites: "Consistent theme: this step marks the first point where sources explicitly expect a pilot to have flown (not just tolerated) genuinely turbulent thermic conditions, not just smooth-day XC."
source.note: If the owner ever decides to honour a soaring route at any step, this is NOT the place to start — mid-B to high-B at least has a source offering one. Here it would be unsupported.

source.cites: "This is the step where sub-class fuzziness (high-B vs low-C overlap) is most clearly documented, so the app should be most cautious about hard EN-letter gating right here."
source.note: Held at 55, identical to all three steps below, so that the whole of this step's extra strictness sits on the Ready edge, in the gates and in the per-option scores — not in pushing more pilots into Not yet. That is the direct application of the sentence quoted above: be cautious about the Ready call, don't become freer with the Not yet call. Below 55 the result is Not yet.

not_yet.framing: A legitimate, successful result — the tool working, not the pilot failing.
not_yet.floor_rule: If either category falls below its floor, the result is Not yet regardless of the total.

source.cites: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note."
source.note: The psychological floor stays at 35, identical to all three steps below, so every reviewed step treats a badly-motivated upgrade the same way. The skills floor rises from 45 to 48 on the asymmetric-risk finding. Both floors are set low so only genuinely poor profiles trip them, not merely mediocre ones. The psychological floor is what stops very strong hands from buying out a poor answer set on motives, social pressure, sunk-cost launching and unexplained incidents — the combination knowledge/disagreements.md point 9 identifies as the one both camps agree is concerning. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/08 is that pilot.

gates.message: While you're still flying under supervision, your wing choice is your instructor's call rather than a questionnaire's. Ask them directly — they can see your flying, and that's worth more than anything this tool can work out.

source.cites: USHPA's syllabus defers wing class to the manufacturer's recommendation rather than naming an EN letter itself.
source.note: A deferral, not a judgement, and the message says so. Conservative per knowledge/disagreements.md point 5. Almost certainly inert three rungs up — flagged in meta.owner_decisions as removable.

gates.message: Under about 25 hours of thermal flying, every published reading of this step puts you a long way below it — the figures range from about 75 hours to over 100, and they're all measuring thermal time specifically. That's the single most useful thing on this page, and it's also the most enjoyable: thermal hours on the wing you already trust, in company, on days that aren't the strongest of the season. Nothing else here moves as much as that does, and almost every other answer improves alongside it.

source.cites: Flybubble's "Which Class?" (industry): roughly 100 hours of thermic flying. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry): 75+ hours of thermic flying, flown regularly. 406 Paragliding (industry): 100+ hours of thermic flying.
source.note: Gated at a THIRD of the lowest published reading, not at any reading, because knowledge/disagreements.md point 2 instructs broad bands over precise figures and point 6 records that the same retailer's two articles disagree with each other here specifically. The band is wider than mid-B to high-B's equivalent gate (under 10 hours there) because the figure it stands below is higher: 25 thermic hours against a 75-hour floor is the same proportional distance as 10 against 50. The message names the range rather than a number, which is the honest framing.

gates.message: Two answers together put this one out of reach for now: under about 50 hours of thermal flying, and not much flying going on at the moment either. Published figures for a first C start at about 75 thermal hours and the two annual figures we found are 50 and 70 hours a year, so you're short on both counts rather than one — and the second is the easier one to change. A season of regular flying moves both at once.

source.cites: The 75-100+ thermic cluster (Flybubble twice, 406 Paragliding), plus the currency framings: paraglidingforum.com's commonly repeated 50+ hours/year rule of thumb and Passion Paragliding's 70 hours/year.
source.note: A combination gate rather than a single-answer one, so a pilot with 40 thermic hours who is flying hard right now is NOT capped — they are held at Nearly ready by the critical_check_floor instead, and told what the figures are. That split matters: knowledge/disagreements.md point 2 records that sources mix cumulative and currency framings without being clear which they mean, so a pilot who is thin on one but strong on the other is in genuinely ambiguous territory, and point 5 says default down rather than out. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/03 is the pilot this clause protects.

gates.message: Get current again on the wing you know before changing wings. A few flights back in easy air and this answer changes on its own.

source.cites: Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry) attaches "flown regularly" to its 75-hour figure; the community rule of thumb at this step is framed annually (50+ hours/year) precisely because currency is treated as the more important measure.
source.note: Gated at the unambiguous case — no flying at all in three months — which is below any reading of any source. Carried forward from all three steps below.

gates.message: This one is about how much flying you're doing right now rather than what you can do. Both figures anyone puts on a first C are annual — around 50 hours a year as a common rule of thumb, 70 in one industry write-up — and monthly flying with under 25 hours in the last year is a long way under either. Nothing about that says anything bad about your flying, and it's the most fixable thing on this page: build the frequency back up on the wing you know and this question answers itself.

source.cites: paraglidingforum.com (community): roughly 50+ flying hours per year before considering EN-C, with currency treated as the more important framing. Passion Paragliding (industry): 70 hours/year. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry): 75+ thermic hours, "flown regularly".
source.note: Widened from mid-B to high-B, where the same gate requires 'less than monthly'. Here 'about monthly' also qualifies when the 12-month total is thin, because the annual figures at this step (50 and 70) are far above what monthly flying produces, where at mid-B to high-B the supporting evidence was qualitative manufacturer copy. Still a combination, so it never fires for a current pilot in a seasonal lull. knowledge/disagreements.md point 10 flags the 70-hour figure as uncorroborated, which is why the gate sits well below both figures rather than at either.

gates.message: This is the one thing at this step that's worth sorting out before anything else, and it's the only place where the published guidance here is clearly more demanding than for the wing you're on. The certification wording for this class assumes precise, deliberate input to recover from a collapse — something you can already do, rather than something to learn on the new wing. By your own answers that reaction hasn't been tested from either direction: no deliberate practice, and no collapse you've caught and flown out yourself. There's also a practical reason not to put it off, made by an instructor who teaches this: wings from about this class upward resist collapsing so well that it gets genuinely hard to stage a realistic one, so the wing you own now is a better one to learn on than the one you're shopping for. Height, a calm day, someone watching the first few — or a course, if you'd rather. Then this answer changes.

source.cites: "This is the first step where 'precise pilot input required for recovery' (the core EN-C certification language) starts being treated by sources as something a pilot needs to already be good at, rather than something to learn on the new wing." USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) requires a demonstrated 50%-asymmetric-collapse recovery with directional control. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor), via knowledge/disagreements.md point 12: from roughly EN-C upward, wings resist collapsing strongly enough that an instructor often can't induce a representative collapse on the wing itself. XC Mag's active-flying piece (industry) places EN-C in the part of the spectrum needing active pilot input rather than self-recovering.
source.note: NEW AT THIS STEP — see meta.design_decisions 'v1-collapse-response-gets-a-gate-of-its-own' and the owner decision about whether it should be a gate at all. Deliberately a combination: self-practised tip folds clear it, and so does having caught a real collapse, so it is not an SIV gate by the back door. The message's last two sentences name a course as one option among others for exactly that reason. BRIEF.md's own gate example is the related but different case, handled by 'collapse_control_lost' below.

gates.message: This is the one worth sorting out before anything else, and worth doing with a coach rather than alone. The class you're looking at is the first one whose certification wording assumes precise input from the pilot to recover — it gives you less time and less help in the same situation, not more. There's a practical argument for doing the work now rather than later, too: the wing you're on is close to the last one you'll own where a collapse can be made to behave realistically enough to practise on. Get the recovery reliable first, then change the wing.

source.cites: "Hard gates: some answers (e.g. frequent collapses they struggle to recover from) cap the result at 'Not yet' regardless of total score." This gate is the brief's own example, almost word for word on the 'repeated_struggle' branch.
source.note: Supported at this boundary by the EN-C certification language treated as a prerequisite rather than a learning goal, and by knowledge/disagreements.md point 12 (Winkler on training feasibility above EN-C), which is what the third sentence states in plain language.

gates.message: Regularly needing several goes, getting pulled around or aborting is worth fixing before adding anything to the wing — a change of glider makes launching harder for a while for everyone, and the ground and the first seconds of flight are where most accidents in this sport happen. Ground handling plus deliberate launch practice moves this faster than anything else.

source.cites: USHPA's 2001 Paragliding Accident Summary (official): around 64% of accidents occurred on the ground or immediately after launch, with accident rates essentially equivalent across P1-P4 pilot ratings. Greg Hamerton via FAI/CIVL (expert): risk rises from unfamiliarity after any gear change.
source.note: Honest flag, carried forward unchanged from mid-B to high-B: this rests on general accident data, not on anything in knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md, which says nothing about launches. Kept as a gate on the worst band only, and deliberately NOT a Ready-blocker, for the same reason. This is a launch-reliability gate, not a ground-handling gate.

gates.message: Someone who has watched you fly has already told you to wait. That beats anything this tool can work out from a questionnaire — and it matters more at this step than most, because this is the boundary the industry argues about most. One instructor writing on safety puts it plainly: the certification letter on a wing is a guideline and doesn't tell you how often that particular wing actually folds. Somebody who knows both your flying and the specific wing is doing work no form can do.

source.cites: Greg Hamerton via FAI/CIVL safety pages (expert) is explicit that the EN/AFNOR letter on its own is only a guideline and doesn't tell a pilot how often a given wing actually collapses in practice — which the step file records as a second, independent expert voice agreeing the letter alone shouldn't be over-trusted at this boundary specifically. knowledge/classification-overview.md: USHPA's syllabus defers the wing-class decision to the manufacturer's recommendation and in practice to the instructor applying it; BRIEF.md requires an instructor recommendation in every result.
source.note: Direct observation outranks self-report. The second half of the message is specific to this step and is sourced rather than rhetorical.

gates.message: One answer is doing a lot of work here: by your own account, your current wing hasn't yet been the thing stopping you. That's the clearest marker in the guidance for this particular step, and it's where the sources are least shy. One industry write-up on this exact transition reckons a large share of pilots already flying C wings moved up chasing performance rather than because they'd run out of wing — and separately, two cross-country-focused sources argue the glide difference between neighbouring classes is usually too small to be what's holding anyone back. Nothing about this is a criticism. It usually means there's performance still sitting in your current wing waiting to be collected, which is the cheapest kind there is.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) states as its own view that roughly half of pilots flying EN-C wings shouldn't yet be on them, having upgraded chasing perceived performance rather than a demonstrated need. Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert) on earned rather than aspirational readiness. Joy Paragliding (industry) and Flybubble's XC Secrets (industry) both argue adjacent-category performance differences are too small to explain being left behind.
source.note: The message says "a large share" rather than repeating the author's 'roughly half' figure, because that is one author's own estimate rather than a study and stating it as a statistic would overstate it. Deliberately a combination gate, never a single-answer one: a pilot who says the wing hasn't limited them yet but is strongly current, well past 100 thermic hours and honest about their motive is NOT capped — they get the 'wing_hasnt_limited_you_yet' suggestion instead. 'want_more_performance' is deliberately absent from the motive list, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 9: Hamerton gives that answer himself and Guschlbauer treats it as legitimate fuel, so it must not help cap anyone.

gates.message: A low-C won't make rough air easier — this is the step where the trade runs most clearly the other way. Its certification class is the first one that assumes precise input from you to recover from a collapse, one instructor describes these wings as pitch-sensitive enough to want the lightest touch, and a coach who writes about the step says the real gain is that the wing tells you more about the air — which is only worth having if you can already use it. What does make rough air easier: thermal hours, active flying, knowing exactly what you'd do if the wing folded, and picking your days. All four are available on the wing you already have, and all four transfer to whatever you fly next.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing transmits genuinely useful extra information, but only pilots who can already read it benefit. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor): EN-C pitch sensitivity demands "the lightest touch". The EN-C certification language: precise pilot input required for recovery. Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz Episode 109 (expert, sports psychologist) names upgrading equipment to compensate for a skill gap rather than closing it, and the step file records her as independently corroborating Passion Paragliding on the same point.
source.note: knowledge/disagreements.md point 9 identifies the combination both camps agree on: an ambition- or comparison-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere. The second clause is wider here than at mid-B to high-B — it adds the collapse_practice branch — because at this step untested collapse response is the specific gap the class's own certification language cares about. The skills threshold is raised from 65 to 70 on the asymmetric-risk finding. It contains no hours clause; thermic hours gate separately on their own evidence. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/08 is the control case: a comparison-flavoured motive with genuinely strong readiness must NOT fire this gate.

gates.message: The goals are fine — they're the reason people keep flying, and nobody should talk you out of them. An X-Alps pilot interviewed on exactly this calls the wish to achieve something the force that drives real progression, and another argues that what keeps the risk of an ambitious plan manageable is trained skill and a genuine fallback, not toning the plan down. The gap here is the groundwork underneath, and almost all of it is learnable on the wing you've got. That's what the suggestions below are about.

source.cites: Recommended handling: ambition itself is legitimate fuel (Guschlbauer via XC Mag's 'The Head Game') and must not be penalised alone; the concerning pattern is ambition paired with thin readiness. Chrigel Maurer via Podz-Glidz Episode 114 (expert), recorded in knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md, is the second voice in the message: trained competence and a genuine fallback plan determine whether risk stays manageable, not the nominal ambition of the plan.
source.note: The skills threshold is held at 55, identical to all three steps below, even though this rubric is otherwise more conservative. That is deliberate: the per-option scores at this step are already harder, so the same 55 is a stricter bar in practice than it is one rung down, and moving the number as well would double-count the tightening. Note that at this step 'longer_xc' is the NORMAL ambition for the class — two official rating ladders expect demonstrated XC flying here — so the second clause is doing all the work, exactly as intended.

gates_deliberately_not_included.reason: Gating at either published figure was considered and rejected. The two figures come from the same retailer's own two articles and disagree with each other (knowledge/disagreements.md points 2 and 6), 406 Paragliding's 100+ is a third version, and the step file instructs treating any figure here as a rough band rather than a cutoff. The unconditional gate sits at a third of the lowest reading; the 25-50 band gates only in combination with thin currency; and the 50-100 band — which contains both readings — is scored at 0.6 and blocks nothing.

The only total-airtime figures at this step (BHPA Advanced Pilot's ~100 hours since the Pilot rating, USHPA P4's 75 hours) are pilot-rating requirements, which knowledge/disagreements.md point 5 says not to treat as EN-letter criteria. Scored at weight 7 and used in no gate.
USHPA P4's 250-flight figure is real and official-adjacent, but it is a pilot-rating requirement and the reused band (150-300) straddles it anyway. Scored at weight 5, gates nothing, blocks nothing.

The clearest new evidence at this step, and deliberately non-gating. knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md's own caveat: "We think it's reasonable for the app to use these as supporting, non-gating signals at this step... rather than as hard, EN-C-specific gates — consistent with how disagreements.md point 5 already recommends treating pilot-rating-ladder evidence." knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 adds Joy Paragliding arguing against tying wing upgrades to kilometres at all, and records that BHPA and FFVL measure different things. Scored at weight 9 and 8; neither is in critical_check_floor.questions.

knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md records that no source ties a ground-handling test to this exact boundary, and knowledge/disagreements.md point 11 says explicitly not to invent a numeric test where none exists. Scored at weight 7 plus 3, and not even a Ready-blocker.

This is the step with the clearest described behavioural change in bar use — routine half bar by EN-C — but the source stating it has uncertain provenance (knowledge/sources.md flags the mirrored class-by-class ladder). Weight raised to 8 and 'never used it' scored down to 0.1, which is the proportionate response to a specific claim from an unverifiable source. Not a gate and not a Ready-blocker.

knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md records one competitive pilot's personal rule — being able to perform reliable full and dynamic stalls on the current wing before moving up — as "a single, informal, non-corroborated signal rather than an established skill bar", and notes he hadn't practised it himself at the time. Not asked, not scored, not gated, and deliberately not surfaced in any suggestion either: putting a stall test in front of a pilot risks reading as encouragement to practise stalls unsupervised, which no source recommends.

Carried forward from config/scoring/a-to-low-b.json's v2 removal of exactly this gate and the two steps since: an injury or reserve ride is not reliably about wing-class readiness. Scored 0.0 on a weight-12 psychological question. Not re-litigated here.

BRIEF.md requires SIV to be optional context only and knowledge/disagreements.md point 1 agrees, including at the steps where the pro-SIV sources are most emphatic. This IS that step — Flybubble recommends it twice, and BHPA's Advanced Pilot rating requires a course — and it is still bonus-only, capped at 2 points, and can never subtract. Note what the new 'collapse_response_entirely_untested' gate deliberately does NOT do: self-practice clears it, so no pilot is ever capped for not having done a course.

knowledge/disagreements.md point 7 records this was searched for specifically across every source, and knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md re-checked it at THIS boundary — where sources do explicitly expect genuinely turbulent thermic air — and still found nothing falsifiable, calling the absence "a genuine, consistent absence across the whole ladder". Not asked, not scored, not gated.

knowledge/disagreements.md point 4 requires 2-liner-ness to be its own gate trigger independent of the EN letter, including for EN-C-certified 2-liners. That belongs to the step above this one: a pilot shopping for an EN-C 2-liner should be assessed on the low-C to high-C/2-liner leg, which asks the cravat-recovery and pitch-control questions. This rubric covers conventional three-line low-C wings and says so rather than silently assuming it.

gate_behaviour.rule: Any fired gate caps the recommendation at Not yet, regardless of score. The numeric score is still shown, with the gate reasons listed above it.
gate_behaviour.evaluation_order: Gates are evaluated first and short-circuit: if any gate fires, the recommendation is Not yet and the threshold rules (category floors, critical_check_floor, unevidenced_core_checks) are not evaluated or reported. This keeps the explanation short and specific rather than piling on reasons.
gate_behaviour.tone_rule: Gate messages state what to work on and why, never that the pilot is unsuitable or has failed. Required by BRIEF.md's safety framing and by docs/design-context.md, which requires a 'not yet' to land as a legitimate, successful result of using the tool. Step-specific addition: no gate message may present the 75-100+ hours range as a single number, and none may claim the high-B/low-C distinction is settled — knowledge/disagreements.md point 3 names it the fuzziest boundary on the ladder.

source.cites: "Hard gates: some answers ... cap the result at 'Not yet' regardless of total score."
source.note: This rubric has 12 gates against 11 at mid-B to high-B, 9 at A to low-B and 8 at low-B to mid-B, so the cap of 3 shown reasons does real work: a genuinely unready pilot can trip four or five. The gates array is ordered so the specific, actionable ones (training status, thermic hours, currency, collapse response, launches, instructor advice) sit above the two combination gates about motive, which read worse when they arrive first. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/06 trips four and is the one to read for whether the stacking reads as a telling-off.

rule_messages.purpose: Pilot-safe copy for the threshold rules, so a pilot held at Nearly ready or pushed to Not yet by a rule gets the same explicit 'here's what's holding this back' as a pilot held by a hard gate. Gates carry their copy on gate.message. Built in from v1, as at the two most recent steps.

lookup.engine_output: app/upgrade/lib/scoreEngine.ts returns ScoreResult.firedRules as an array of strings in one of two shapes: '<rule_id>' (only 'conservative_backstop' today) or '<rule_id>:<question_id_or_category>' (everything else).
lookup.structure: Two flat maps. 'by_rule' is keyed by the EXACT fired-rule string, so no parsing or templating is needed at render time. 'fallback_by_rule_id' is keyed by the part before the colon, and exists only so a future question added to critical_check_floor.questions (or a future answer added to unevidenced_core_checks.answers) can never render a missing message.
algorithm: 3. if still not found: render nothing for that rule. Never render the raw fired-rule string, a rule id, or a question id to a pilot.
lookup.render_as: Each entry has a plain prose 'message' string, exactly like gate.message, intended for the same 'What's holding this back' card and the same paragraph treatment. There is deliberately no per-message heading field: rules can fire together, and two headings in one card reads badly.
lookup.division_of_labour_with_suggestions: Every answer band that can trip a threshold rule also triggers a suggestion in config/suggestions/high-b-to-low-c.json, and both appear on the same result screen. The split is: the rule message says WHY this one answer is holding the result and what the guidance actually says; the suggestion says HOW to move it. The pairs are thermic_airtime/build_thermic_hours, collapse_practice/collapse_practice_now, wing_limiting_evidence/wing_hasnt_limited_you_yet, active_piloting/active_piloting_light_touch, thermal_turn_control/thermal_skills_drill, response_when_rough/nerves_are_not_the_problem, flying_frequency/improve_currency, collapse_experience/post_collapse_support, reading_the_day/reading_the_day_drill, reserve_familiarity/reserve_practice, and unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_control/thermalling_untested. If any of those suggestions is retired, re-read the paired message — a 'there's a suggestion below' pointer with nothing below it is the failure mode to watch for.
lookup.multiplicity: critical_check_floor breaks on its first failing question, so at most ONE 'critical_check_floor:*' string can appear in firedRules, and the question it names is the first failure in thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.questions order, not necessarily the worst one — which is why that list is deliberately ordered. Same for unevidenced_core_checks. The two category-floor rules are independent and can both appear. Gates and rules are mutually exclusive: gates short-circuit, so firedRules is always empty when firedGates is non-empty.
lookup.internal_fields: The 'source' block on each entry is provenance for the owner and reviewer only. Only 'message' is ever rendered.

display.order: The order the engine emits them, which is already roughly most-to-least specific: category floors, then critical_check_floor, then unevidenced_core_checks, then conservative_backstop.
display.why_two_and_not_three: gate_behaviour.max_gate_reasons_shown is 3, but several rules can fire together on the Nearly ready path, and these are softer and more overlapping reasons than gates. Nearly ready means 'close' — listing five things reads as a telling-off and contradicts the result. Two keeps it specific; the suggestions list carries the rest.
display.tone_rule: Same rule as gate_behaviour.tone_rule. Step-specific additions: (a) messages MAY name the 75-to-100-plus hours RANGE, and must present it as a range rather than a figure, attributing it ('the published figures run from', 'the guidance lands somewhere between') rather than stating it as this tool's own bar; (b) no message may imply the high-B/low-C distinction is settled — where it is relevant, say plainly that the industry argues about it; (c) no message may repeat the 'roughly half of C pilots' estimate as a statistic.

source.cites: The brief requires the result to be transparent and rule-based rather than a black box, and requires the 'Not yet' framing to be a legitimate result rather than a failure.
source.note: docs/design-context.md's safety guard is the binding constraint on the two not_yet_category_floor messages. No wording from that document, and none of its terminology, appears in any message here.

critical_check_floor:thermic_airtime.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the number the guidance for this step actually measures: thermal hours specifically. The published figures run from about 75 hours to over 100 — one retailer's own two articles say 75 in one and 100 in the other, so it's a range rather than a line — and you're between 25 and 50. Worth being clear what this isn't. It isn't a comment on your flying, and ridge or coastal hours aren't wasted hours. It's that every source that puts a number on this particular step counts thermal time, because that's the air these wings are described for. The suggestions below are about adding the hours without making a project of it — and this is the one answer on the page that drags most of the others along with it when it improves.

source.cites: Flybubble's "Which Class?" (industry): ~100 hours of thermic flying. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry): 75+ hours of thermic flying, flown regularly. 406 Paragliding (industry): 100+ hours of thermic flying. The step file's consensus read treats any figure as a rough band rather than a cutoff.
source.note: Reached by the 25_50 band only: under_25 is caught earlier by a gate, and 50_100 scores 0.6 and passes. The 'range rather than a line' sentence is load-bearing honesty per knowledge/disagreements.md points 2 and 6. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/03 renders this message.

critical_check_floor:collapse_practice.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the one place this step genuinely asks more of you than the wing you're on does. Pulling and releasing tip folds yourself with height is real practice and it counts — one rung down it would have been plenty. Here the certification wording for the class assumes precise, deliberate input to recover from a bigger collapse, which the guidance treats as something to arrive with rather than learn on the new wing. There's a practical reason to do the rest now rather than after: an instructor who teaches this points out that wings from about this class upward resist collapsing so well that it's hard to stage a realistic one, so your current wing is close to the best one you'll own for the job. Wingovers, a spiral you can enter gently and exit tidily, a bigger asymmetric with someone watching — the suggestion below has the order to do it in.

source.cites: The EN-C certification language (precise pilot input required for recovery) treated by this step's sources as a skill to arrive with rather than learn. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry) on ongoing wingover, spiral and asymmetric practice. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor) via knowledge/disagreements.md point 12 on training feasibility above EN-C.
source.note: Reached by 'some_self_practice' (0.45) in practice: 'no practice' and 'theory only' usually trip the 'collapse_response_entirely_untested' gate instead, and reach this rule only for a pilot who has separately caught and flown out a real collapse. The message opens by crediting the self-practice, deliberately — this answer was full marks' worth two rungs down and the pilot deserves to know the standard moved, not to be told they did nothing.

critical_check_floor:wing_limiting_evide.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the point the guidance for this step is least shy about: by your own account, your current wing hasn't clearly been the thing stopping you yet. One industry piece written specifically about this transition argues that a large share of pilots already on C wings moved up chasing performance rather than because they'd run out of wing, and two cross-country-focused sources separately argue the glide difference between neighbouring classes is usually too small to be what's holding anyone back. None of that is a criticism, and it's a good problem to have: it usually means there's performance still sitting in your current wing waiting to be collected, which is the cheapest kind there is. The suggestion below has a concrete way to test whether that's true over the next few flights.

source.cites: Passion Paragliding (industry) on upgrading without demonstrated need at this exact transition; Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert) on earned rather than aspirational readiness; Joy Paragliding (industry) and Flybubble's XC Secrets (industry) on adjacent-category performance differences being small.
source.note: Reached by 'not really' and 'I've wondered but couldn't point to a flight'. A pilot answering 'not really' alongside thin skills, a comparison-flavoured motive or thin thermic hours is caught earlier by the 'aspirational_rather_than_demonstrated' gate, so this rule mostly fires for the otherwise-strong pilot — which is why the tone is explicitly non-critical. Per display.tone_rule, the author's 'roughly half' estimate is reported as 'a large share' rather than as a statistic.

critical_check_floor:active_piloting.message: One thing is holding this back: what your hands do when the air gets bumpy. This is the check that moves most between the wing you're on and the one you're looking at. An instructor who specialises in steering technique describes wings in this class as pitch-sensitive enough to want the lightest touch, and an industry piece on active flying places them in the part of the range that needs real pilot input rather than sorting itself out. Hands that stop moving, or brakes held in tight, are both habits worth unlearning on a wing that forgives them — and the forgiving wing is the one you already own. The suggestion below has the drill, which works best in light, friendly bumps rather than on the big days.

source.cites: Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor): EN-C wings have pitch sensitivity demanding "the lightest touch". XC Mag's active-flying piece (industry): a spectrum from school wings stable through major collapses, through self-recovering intermediate wings, to competition-style wings needing active pilot input, with EN-C in the more demanding part.
source.note: 'Hands still', 'grip tight' and 'try to react' reach this rule. 'I work the brakes to keep the pressure even' scores 0.6 and passes, though it is marked down from 0.7 one rung below and 0.9 two rungs below — that is a scoring change, not a block, and the 'active_piloting_light_touch' suggestion is where the refinement is explained.

critical_check_floor:thermal_turn_contro.message: One thing is holding this back: thermalling that works but isn't yet under your control — wide turns, losing the core. It carries more weight here than anywhere below, for two reasons. Every source that puts a number on this step counts thermal hours specifically, so thermalling is the activity the class exists for rather than one skill among many. And a coach who writes about exactly this step makes the sharper point: what you actually buy at this level is a wing that tells you more about the air, and that's only worth having if you can already act on what it's telling you. Otherwise you get a bit more glide and some more speed, and miss the rest. The suggestion below has specific things to drill.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing starts transmitting genuinely useful extra information about the air, but only pilots who can already read and interpret it benefit; pilots who can't will "notice a better glide and some more speed" and miss everything else. The thermic-hours figures from Flybubble (twice) and 406 Paragliding make thermic flying the measured activity.
source.note: 'Not confident with it yet' and 'wide turns, losing the core' reach this rule. 'I mostly soar or glide rather than thermal' scores 0.5, exactly on the minimum, so it passes here and is handled by 'unevidenced_core_checks' instead.

critical_check_floor:response_when_rough.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't nerves — everyone's heart rate climbs in rough air and that part is normal, not a weakness. It's what comes next: tightening up and waiting it out rather than carrying on flying the wing. That answer carries more weight at this step than any other single question, and that's not our judgement — it's what the pilots who fly both these classes point at. They argue endlessly about whether a steady low-C or a lively high-B actually feels calmer in bad air, and the one thing that disagreement settles is that your own sense of control in rough air tells you more than the letter on the wing does. What you do under load is a habit rather than a personality trait, so it builds. Until it feels different, the more forgiving wing is the right one to be building it on — there's a suggestion below on how.

source.cites: "The community thread on 'High End Bs vs. Low EN Cs' shows pilots disagreeing about which actually feels calmer in bad air... This argues for the app weighting the pilot's own reported comfort/control in rough air fairly heavily at this step, rather than leaning only on the EN letter." paraglidingforum.com (community) pairs its annual-hours rule of thumb with "the more important qualitative test of feeling in control in rough air, not just calm air". XC Mag's 'The Head Game' (industry/expert, Thomas Theurillat) frames readiness as challenge matched to honest self-assessed skill.
source.note: Written about behaviour under load, not about feeling afraid, and deliberately does not reassure a hesitant pilot toward upgrading — the hesitation here is well-founded and the message says the forgiving wing is the right one for now. Required by docs/design-context.md; none of its terminology is used.

critical_check_floor:flying_frequency.message: One thing is holding this back: flying about once a month. Both figures anyone puts on a first C are annual rather than lifetime — around 50 hours a year as a common rule of thumb among pilots, 70 in one industry write-up — and monthly flying doesn't get close to either, however many hours are behind you. There's no agreed number and these aren't strong sources, which is why this holds the result rather than capping it. Two or three times a month, in whatever conditions you can get, changes this answer and several others with it.

source.cites: paraglidingforum.com (community, explicitly used only to show rough practitioner consensus rather than as a citable criterion): roughly 50+ flying hours per year before considering EN-C. Passion Paragliding (industry): 70 hours/year. Flybubble's "Reducing Risk" (industry): "flown regularly".
source.note: Only 'about once a month' with a reasonable 12-month total reaches this rule: thinner combinations are caught earlier by the 'no_recent_flying' and 'occasional_pilot_profile' gates. The message says 'these aren't strong sources' deliberately — one is a forum rule of thumb the knowledge base refuses to cite as a criterion, the other is flagged as uncorroborated in knowledge/disagreements.md point 10.

critical_check_floor:collapse_experience.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't that you froze — that's what most people do the first time, and it's the normal starting point rather than a character flaw. It's that the wing sorted itself out without you, so the reaction hasn't been tested. That matters more at this step than any below it: this is the first class whose certification wording assumes precise input from the pilot to recover, which the guidance treats as something to arrive with rather than learn on the new wing. The good news is that it's trainable and you're holding the right wing for it — an instructor who teaches this points out that wings from about the class you're shopping for upward resist collapsing so well that staging a realistic one gets difficult. There's a suggestion below, and a second one about doing it with someone watching.

source.cites: The EN-C certification language treated as a prerequisite rather than a learning goal. USHPA P4 (official via AirAddict) requires a demonstrated 50%-asymmetric recovery with directional control. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor) via knowledge/disagreements.md point 12 on training feasibility above EN-C.
source.note: Only 'I froze and the wing recovered on its own' reaches this rule, and only for a pilot who HAS practised at least self-folds — otherwise the 'collapse_response_entirely_untested' gate fires first. 'Lost control' and 'happened a few times and I still struggle' fire the 'collapse_control_lost' gate. 'Never' scores exactly 0.5 and passes.

critical_check_floor:reading_the_day.message: One thing is holding this back: reading the day being about half right so far. At the rungs below this one that answer passes — it's an honest, normal place to be. The reason it holds the result here is a specific argument from a coach who writes about this exact step: what you're really buying is a wing that gives you more information about the air, and that only pays if you can already interpret it. Day-judgement is the same skill at a bigger scale, and this is the step where the flying starts happening further from home, at sites you know less well, on days you chose yourself. It's also one of the cheapest things on your list to move — it builds from attention and conversation as much as from airtime. The suggestion below has the drill.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): the EN-C step is where a wing transmits genuinely useful extra information about the air, and only pilots who can already read and interpret that information benefit. USHPA's P4 syllabus (official via AirAddict) expects 5 flights at each of 5 different sites in Intermediate-level conditions, 3 of them inland.
source.note: Both 'I mostly go when other people say it's good' (0.1) and 'right about half the time' (0.45) reach this rule — the second is new at this step, and the message names that change rather than hiding it. This is the one bar mid-B to high-B deliberately declined to raise, so the justification has to be visible: see that question's disagreement_note. A reviewer who disagrees should put 'sometimes_right' back to 0.5.

critical_check_floor:reserve_familiarity.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the quickest on the whole list to fix: not being certain you could find the reserve handle in a hurry. Two minutes in a hang check changes this answer permanently. It's the only item here that takes minutes rather than seasons, which is the one reason a single answer about it can hold an otherwise strong result. There's a suggestion below on how to practise it.

source.cites: USHPA P2 (official) includes reserve-deployment and PLF knowledge among its required skills.
source.note: Cross-referenced from three steps below: knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md names no reserve criterion. Kept as a Ready-blocker on knowledge/disagreements.md point 5's conservative default, and flagged in this file as the weakest-sourced member of critical_check_floor.questions. The message avoids claiming a standard and leans on how cheap the fix is, which is the honest basis for it. Only 'I'm not completely sure' reaches it; 'I know where it is but have never practised' scores exactly 0.5 and passes.

unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_con.message: One thing is unevidenced rather than weak. You've said you mostly soar or glide rather than thermal, so the main thing this step is measured by hasn't been tested — and it isn't counted against you, it scores as neutral. But every source that puts a number on this step counts thermal hours specifically, this is the first rung where the guidance expects you to have actually flown genuinely rough thermic air rather than just put up with it, and the two national training systems this step borrows from add cross-country flying and a range of sites on top. So this result doesn't move just because your plans are local: there isn't a reading of the guidance here that a soaring-only pilot clears. That's worth knowing plainly rather than finding out later. There's a suggestion below about what a low-C would and wouldn't give you for the flying you've described.

source.cites: "Consistent theme: this step marks the first point where sources explicitly expect a pilot to have flown (not just tolerated) genuinely turbulent thermic conditions, not just smooth-day XC." All three industry hours figures measure thermic flying; USHPA P4 and BHPA Advanced Pilot add site variety and cross-country distance.
source.note: The pilot-facing form of thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.exemptions_deliberately_empty. Unlike at mid-B to high-B, there is no competing source offering a soaring route to decline, so the message can state the absence plainly rather than naming a disagreement. Paired with the 'thermalling_untested' and 'local_plans_and_this_wings_purpose' suggestions, which carry the practical half.

ready_category_floor:skills.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the skills and experience half of it isn't carrying its own weight yet. The two halves are scored separately on purpose, so that good judgement and honest motives can't stand in for airtime and handling, or the other way round. At this step in particular the two halves are nearly equal in the total, which is why one of them can hold the result on its own. What's holding this back is on the skills side, and the suggestions below are the specific parts of it.

source.cites: SAHPA's conservative-by-default pattern: when evidence is ambiguous, default toward 'Not yet' or 'Nearly ready' rather than 'Ready'.
source.note: Names the category rather than the floor value; the number would be false precision, since thresholds.ready.source records these figures as synthesised rather than sourced. tests/personas/high-b-to-low-c/07 renders this message — the pilot with excellent judgement whose flying is all at one site.

ready_category_floor:psychological.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the mindset and motivation half of it is sitting well below the skills half. Those are scored separately on purpose and at this step they count for nearly as much as each other: what you expect the new wing to actually do, what you're working on, how the call gets made on a marginal day or after a long drive, and what you do when it gets rough all matter here as much as hours and handling. This is also the step where the published guidance is most direct about it — the most pointed piece written about this exact transition is about motives rather than skills. It's usually the quicker half to move.

source.cites: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note." Plus knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#psychological--mindset-factors: Passion Paragliding is the most pointed source in the knowledge base on this exact transition and is about motives, not hours; Yvonne Dathe corroborates independently from a sports-psychology angle.
source.note: 'Usually the quicker half to move' is deliberate: these are answers that change with a conversation and some reading, not with another fifty hours — and saying so keeps the message from reading as a verdict on the pilot's character.

not_yet_category_floor:skills.message: Whatever the total came out at, the skills and experience answers point the same way: more flying on the wing you've already got is the useful next step, rather than a different wing. That's a normal place to be, and this rung in particular is one most pilots spend a couple of seasons on — it's also the one the industry argues about most, which is a reason to take your time rather than a reason to hurry. It's the most fixable half of the picture too: thermal hours, active flying, collapse practice, reading the day, getting to a few more sites. Every one of them moves this, and every one of them transfers to whatever you fly next, so none of that time is spent waiting.

source.cites: "Hard gates: some answers ... cap the result at 'Not yet' regardless of total score." The category floors are the same idea applied to a whole category rather than a single answer.
source.note: Tone is bound by docs/design-context.md's safety guard: this must land as a legitimate, useful result, never as a failure. The 'couple of seasons' framing is supported by knowledge/disagreements.md point 13 (every source addressing progression pace assumes one rung at a time) and point 10 (a community rule of thumb of 150-200 hours per wing-class step). The 'argues about it most' clause is knowledge/disagreements.md point 3.

not_yet_category_floor:psychological.message: This one isn't about your hands. The answers about why the change, what you expect it to give you, what you're working on, how decisions get made on a day you're unsure about or after a long drive, and what's happened in the last year are where this result comes from — and here they count for nearly as much as hours and handling, by design. None of that is a judgement on you as a pilot. It's also the half the guidance for this step is most direct about: the most pointed thing written about this exact transition is about why pilots move up, not about what they can do, and it names comparing yourself to the people you fly with as one of the two motives that go wrong most often. It's the half worth working through first, and it usually takes a conversation with someone who knows your flying rather than another fifty hours in the air.

source.cites: Recommended handling: motivation is a genuinely scored input, and the diagnostic combination both camps agree on is an ambition- or comparison-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere. knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#psychological--mindset-factors: Passion Paragliding names ego and peer pressure explicitly as the drivers at this transition; Yvonne Dathe corroborates independently.
source.note: This is the more serious of the two floors — it produces Not yet rather than Nearly ready — so the tone constraint from docs/design-context.md is strictest here. 'None of that is a judgement on you as a pilot' is load-bearing and should not be cut: the answers that trip this floor (comparison-driven motives, launching under social pressure, pressing on after a long drive, unexplained near misses) are the ones most likely to read as character criticism if stated plainly. The message names the question areas without quoting any specific answer back at the pilot, and does not repeat the 'roughly half of C pilots' estimate.

conservative_backstop.message: A few of the main questions were left blank, so there isn't quite enough here to put the result any higher than this. Nothing is counted against you for skipping them — when the tool doesn't know, it assumes the more cautious answer rather than the generous one. If you'd like a sharper result, going back and filling those in is the whole fix.

source.cites: SAHPA's design pattern of defaulting an unregistered glider to the most demanding category unless a lower class is actively registered. Applied here as: when the evidence is incomplete, default down rather than up.
source.note: Framed as missing information, not as a penalty, and ends with the action. Fires when more than two 'core' questions are unanswered. It can fire alongside other rules, which is one reason display.max_rule_reasons_shown is 2 — but the engine emits it last, so if it is cut by that limit the pilot still sees the more specific reason.

rule_messages.fallback_purpose: Entries under 'fallback_by_rule_id' are used only when 'by_rule' has no entry for the exact fired-rule string — i.e. when a question is added to thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.questions, or an answer to thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.answers, without per-case copy being written. They are intentionally vaguer than the per-question messages and should be treated as a bug signal, not a design target: if one of these ever renders, write the specific message.

critical_check_floor.message: One specific check for this step came out low, and a single weak answer in that group holds the result here even when everything else is strong — that's deliberate, so a good overall average can't cover one thin safety skill. The suggestions below name the one it was and what moves it.

source.cites: Every member of this group is individually sourced at this boundary — see thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.source.

unevidenced_core_checks.message: One of the checks for this step hasn't been tested rather than failed. That isn't counted against you — it scores as neutral — but the guidance treats it as something to have demonstrated before moving to a wing that gives you more information and less margin, so the result stays here until there's something to go on. The suggestions below cover how to test it while the stakes are low.

source.cites: SAHPA's pattern of defaulting to the most conservative category unless a lower one is actively evidenced.

ready_category_floor.message: Your total is in the ready band, but one of the two halves of it — skills and experience, or mindset and motivation — is sitting well below the other. They're scored separately on purpose so neither can stand in for the other. The suggestions below are about the half that's holding it.

source.cites: SAHPA's conservative-by-default pattern: default toward 'Nearly ready' rather than 'Ready' where the evidence is uneven.

not_yet_category_floor.message: One of the two halves of this — skills and experience, or mindset and motivation — came out low enough that it decides the result on its own, whatever the total says. That's a normal result and a useful one: it means there's a specific half to work on rather than a vague sense of not being ready. The suggestions below are the concrete version.

source.cites: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note." Plus docs/design-context.md's requirement that a 'not yet' land as a legitimate result rather than a failure.

always_output.instructor_recommendation: Whatever this says, run it past an instructor or coach who has seen you fly — and test-fly the specific wing before you buy it. That matters more at this step than at any below it, because this is the boundary the industry argues about most: one manufacturer calls its own entry-level C a small step up from its best-known high-B, pilots disagree about which of the two actually feels calmer in bad air, and an instructor writing on safety points out that the letter on a wing doesn't tell you how often that particular wing folds. The specific wing and the specific pilot both matter here more than the category does.
always_output.disclaimer: This is a self-assessment tool based on published guidance from national associations, manufacturers, retailers and instructors. It isn't an instructor, it can't see you fly, and it isn't a safety clearance. Wing choice is your responsibility and your instructor's advice always comes first.
always_output.methodology_note: This step has more published guidance behind it than any rung below — and the guidance disagrees with itself. The hours figures for a first C range from about 75 to over 100, all measuring thermal flying specifically, and one retailer's own two articles give different numbers; the two annual figures we found are 50 and 70 hours a year; and the industry doesn't agree that "high B" and "low C" are meaningfully different categories at all. So nothing here is gated on any one number: the hours questions use broad bands, and the result leans on demonstrated handling, currency and collapse response instead. Two questions appear at this step for the first time — how many different sites you've flown and how much cross-country you've done — because two national training systems ask for both at around this stage. They're scored but can't hold your result on their own, because they come from pilot-rating schemes rather than from anything written about wing classes, and one cross-country source argues kilometres flown says little about which wing to fly. Where the sources disagreed we took the more cautious reading, for one specific reason the pilots who fly these wings keep repeating: getting onto a C too early costs more than staying on a B too long. Every weight and gate links back to the criterion it came from.
